items.title: 2027: INEC moves to address electoral risks in Ebonyi
items.description: By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) in Ebonyi State has intensified efforts to identify and address potential risks that could disrupt the conduct of the 2027 general elections. The move followed a workshop on Electoral Risk Management organised at the commission’s headquarters in Abakaliki for stakeholders, including media representatives, security agencies and local government electoral officers. Participants identified potential threats to the elections, including snatching and destruction of electoral materials, abduction of election officials and the inaccessibility of some villages and communities. Speaking at the workshop, INEC Administrative Secretary in Ebonyi State, Mrs Joan Onyibor, said the exercise was timely given the proximity of the January and February 2027 elections. She explained that electoral risk management provided a structured and proactive approach to identifying, assessing, monitoring and mitigating threats that could compromise the electoral process. According to her, such risks could include security threats, political tensions, misinformation, environmental challenges, logistical constraints and other operational difficulties. Onyibor warned that failure to identify and address the risks could disrupt electoral activities, endanger voters and election officials, and undermine public confidence in the electoral process. Declaring the workshop open, the Resident Electoral Commissioner (REC) in Ebonyi State, Mrs Pauline Ugochi Onyeka, commended the Head of Planning and Monitoring, Mrs Mercy Amechi-Okorie, for organising the programme for stakeholders. Onyeka said strengthening the electoral risk management framework had become increasingly important as the 2027 elections approached. “We must move beyond responding to challenges only after they emerge and adopt a proactive approach that allows us to anticipate risks and address them before they develop into serious threats,” she said. She added that the workshop was designed to improve stakeholders’ understanding of electoral risk management, build institutional capacity and strengthen their ability to identify, document and report potential threats across different locations. The REC stressed that effective electoral risk management depended on close cooperation and timely information-sharing among INEC offices, security agencies, civil society organisations, the media and other stakeholders. “No institution can manage every electoral risk effectively on its own,” Onyeka said, calling for a coordinated approach to strengthen preparedness and response mechanisms. She said collaboration among stakeholders would help improve the security and integrity of the electoral process ahead of the 2027 general elections. The post 2027: INEC moves to address electoral risks in Ebonyi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Accidente de trenes en Toledo: última hora y reacciones en directo | Asciende a 69 el número de fallecidos en el accidente ferroviario de Urda
items.description: El presidente de Castilla-La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, ha informado este jueves de que el número de fallecidos por la tragedia en Urda (Toledo) asciende a 69. Como consecuencia del accidente, alrededor de 200 personas resultaron heridas. De ellas, 50 continúan ingresadas en hospitales de Castilla-La Mancha, mientras que los servicios sanitarios de Madrid han atendido a casi un centenar. El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, que se ha desplazado a Urda para participar en la reunión del Cecopi, ha asegurado que se “reforzará la seguridad” para que no vuelva a ocurrir una tragedia ferroviaria como esta. Del otro lado, el líder del Partido Popular, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, ha criticado que el ministro de Transporte, Óscar Puente, “echara la culpa” del accidente a un operador de Atocha y lo considera una “frivolidad”. Los Reyes tienen previsto visitar a los heridos en el Hospital Universitario de Toledo a lo largo del día. El secretario general del Sindicato Español de Maquinistas y Ayudantes Ferroviarios, Diego Martín, ha tachado de “alarmante e irrespetuoso” que se filtren los “audios sesgados” del centro de control que muestran el error del responsable de Atocha. El secretario general de los maquinistas españoles ha denunciado también “que cada vez se trabaja más con sistemas degradados”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: 117 ans après la disparition de Seydina Limamou Laye
items.description: Après 26 ans de mission auprès des hommes et des djinns, en tant que Mahdi Mountazar (Bien-Guidé), à la suite de son Appel lancé le 1er Chaa’ban 1301 H (25 mai 1884), Seydina Limamou Laye s’éteignit à l’âge de 66 ans, le 29 octobre 1909, correspondant au 14 Chawwal 1327 de l’hégire. La date du 29 octobre du calendrier grégorien constitue un marqueur pour la communauté layène, car elle coïncide avec le rappel à Dieu de Seydina Limamou Laye. C’était peu avant l’aube du vendredi 14 Chawwal 1327 de l’hégire que le Saint Maître rendit son dernier souffle, après avoir prononcé la formule d’unicité et de foi : « J’atteste qu’il n’y a de Dieu qu’Allah, qu’Il n’a point d’associé, et j’atteste que Mohammed est Son serviteur et Son Envoyé », rapporte Cheikh Makhtar Lô. Ce dernier, dans son livre Busrâ al-Muhhibîn wa Tayqîz al-Jâhilîn, ou « Joie des amis et réveil des égarés », retrace les derniers instants de la vie de Seydina Limamou Laye. Selon lui, vers le milieu de la nuit, le guide ordonna à ses épouses d’aller se coucher. Peu de personnes parmi les femmes restèrent avec lui. Au fil de la nuit, suivant l’évolution de la pleine lune dans le ciel, Seydina Limamou ne cessa de demander : « À quel moment de la nuit sommes-nous ? », s’interrogeant incessamment. À chaque fois, il enleva les vêtements qu’il portait et dit : « Donnez-les en aumône à telle personne. » Il en porta d’autres et se recoucha. Il répéta ce geste jusqu’à ce que la trajectoire de la lune se situe entre le zénith et l’horizon, moment où son âme quitta son corps. En amont de cette fatidique échéance, Seydina Limamou Laye était resté alité pendant 13 jours. Les prémices remontaient au milieu du mois de Ramadan de la même année. Selon Cheikh Makhtar Lô, il savait que la fin était proche, car, au milieu du mois de jeûne, il leur ordonna d’écrire des lettres à destination de toutes les parties du pays pour demander à ses fidèles de venir assister à la fête de Korité. Le jour de l’Aïd, Seydina laissait entendre : « Si vous ne vous dépêchez pas, je ne pourrai pas me rendre au lieu de la prière, car je suis presque un mort », avant d’ajouter : « Si l’on disait qu’un mort peut diriger une prière, cela paraîtrait étonnant. Je le jure par Dieu, je suis un mort. » À l’approche de son rappel à Dieu, Seydina Limamou ne cessa de réaffirmer sa mission prophétique, lancée à l’âge de 40 ans. Il se disait être la réincarnation du prophète Mohammed (PSL), dans sa célèbre expression wolof : « Mana Demb, mana Tay », c’est-à-dire : « Ce fut moi hier, ce fut moi aujourd’hui. » Loin de toute dichotomie, il rappelait que le Mahdi n’était personne d’autre que le prophète lui-même. Dans un hadith, le prophète disait que le Mahdi suivrait ses traces et ne s’en dévierait pas. Partant de cette affirmation, Cheikh Makhtar Lô s’interroge : qui peut suivre les traces du prophète sans en dévier, si ce n’est le prophète lui-même ? D’ailleurs, Seydina Limamou Laye aimait dire : « Si vous voyez en moi un comportement ou des actes qui s’écartent de ceux de Mohammed, sachez que je ne suis pas le vrai Mahdi. » Au-delà du fait qu’il était illettré, Seydina Limamou Laye lança son Appel à l’âge de 40 ans, resta alité pendant 13 jours avant son rappel à Dieu et attendit 3 jours avant d’être enterré. À l’occasion de son rappel à Dieu, son fils aîné et successeur confirmateur, Seydina Issa Rohou Lahi, était en exil à Ngakham depuis 1906. Son retour n’eut lieu que le dimanche 31 octobre 1909, à la gare de Yarakh (Hann). Ce n’est que le lendemain, lundi 1er novembre, qu’il présida la première prière mortuaire de son père, tel que prédit par les textes sacrés : le Messie officiera la première prière mortuaire du Mahdi et régnera pendant 40 ans à la tête de la Oummah. Mohamed DIENE

items.title: How to Lose Texas
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts For years, Latino voters reliably voted for Democratic presidential candidates, in many cases by double-digit margins. Then in 2024, they roughly split their vote, becoming a key swing group for Donald Trump’s return to power—perhaps because they liked his style, or they perceived him as an outsider, or they agreed that the border had gotten out of control. In 2026, though, polls are indicating that they may be over him. One of the best test cases for the shift is the Rio Grande Valley in Texas, right along the southern U.S. border. The area was a Democratic stronghold for decades before it went for Trump in 2024. It’s dominated by working-class Latinos, mostly Mexican American. In the immediate post-pandemic years, the area saw an unprecedented number of illegal border crossings, and voters seemingly punished Joe Biden for the chaos. But their desire for order wasn’t a desire for what the administration delivered: ICE raids that have seemed random, law-abiding friends and family who have been deported, and treatment that has felt dehumanizing. The Atlantic staff writer Nick Miroff traveled to the Rio Grande Valley and talked with people whose family members or employees had been targeted by ICE. He talked with politicians and candidates about how they’ve shifted their strategies, and he talked with people who had the same concerns as any middle-class American, about how much everything costs now. On Radio Atlantic , Miroff discusses the wild political swings in the Rio Grande Valley and what they might reveal about the statewide Texas races and the Latino vote in the rest of the country. The following is a transcript of the episode: Hanna Rosin: One of the big surprises of the 2024 presidential election was how much Latino voters had shifted right. A bloc that has voted Democratic consistently, for decades, had helped reelect Donald Trump, which led to lots of gloating from Republicans about their new diverse coalition and angst from Democrats about what they’d gotten wrong. Well, the punditry came too soon. In the upcoming midterms, it seems like Latinos are shifting back again, which you can see very clearly in Texas and especially in the Rio Grande Valley. Nick Miroff: So the RGV, the Rio Grande Valley, is to me one of the most fascinating parts of the United States. And this is an area that is more than 90 percent Hispanic. Rosin: Staff writer Nick Miroff, who covers immigration, recently did some reporting in South Texas. Miroff: Got the sound of a guy welding, welding a cattle trailer. [ Music ] Miroff: This is an area that has been a Democratic Party stronghold for decades—or was up until this past election. And that was a real seismic shift in politics, and it was fundamental to the kind of coalition that Trump was able to put together in 2024. And I wanted to go back and talk to voters there now to see how they’re feeling about the way the country is going, about their lives, and how they plan to vote in the midterms. Miroff: Are you gonna vote for Talarico? Benny Melendez: Yeah, definitely. Miroff: All Democrats? Melendez: All Democrat, yeah. Rosin: This is Radio Atlantic . I’m Hanna Rosin. Today on the show, we are taking a closer look at the Rio Grande Valley, because it could reveal what’s about to happen in Texas more broadly, but also possibly the whole country. For next week’s midterms, Latinos might end up being the critical voting bloc. But here’s the thing: What Nick learned from visiting the Rio Grande Valley—what maybe everybody should have learned from the last presidential election—is that the mistake is to think of them as any kind of unified ethnic voting bloc at all. In the story he wrote , Nick, for example, rechristened them the “Big-Ass Truck Vote” because love for big trucks and the high cost of filling up their tanks seemed higher on the list of motivators than undying party loyalty. Anyway, back to the valley. [ Music ] Rosin: Now, I’ve never been there. What does it look like? Like, can you just describe it? Is it rural? Is it farmland? What are people doing? How close is it to Mexico? How big is it? I’m just curious to get a picture in my head. Miroff: Yeah. Well, the first thing I think is that calling it a valley is a bit of a misnomer. It’s more like this is the part, you know, where the Rio Grande meets the Gulf of Mexico, and it’s really like a floodplain, so it’s flat. It’s very hot and muggy. And this was an area that was a big agricultural region for generations, but over the past several decades has been changing rapidly, predominantly after the North American Free Trade Agreement went into effect in 1994. These towns—Brownsville, McAllen—became kind of operational-logistics hubs for trade with Mexico. And so for many years, this has been an area that immigrants, as well as, you know, Hispanic Americans living in South Texas viewed, I think, as a place of opportunity, where the jobs were plentiful and where people could live a kind of—you know, aspire to a middle-class life. This is an area where you have big, wide streets and brand-new subdivisions, but also many pockets of poverty, communities known as colonias that are kind of on unincorporated land. Miroff: We’re in a colonia —lots of fences; lots of yard ornaments, beware of the dog signs, trampolines, junked cars. Miroff: It’s really an area that’s been transformed, in particular, over the past, I would say, about 15 years by migration from Mexico and drug violence in northern Mexico, because the cartel wars sent so many middle-class and even upper-middle-class, you know, Mexicans fleeing for somewhere safe. And a lot of them went to the Rio Grande Valley, and they brought this kind of new dynamism to that area. But as one of the candidates that I spent time with talked about, you know, it also brought a kind of integration with a lot more mixed-status families. Rosin: Right. Okay, I think I’m getting the picture, and it’s an interesting picture, and now I see why you went there. It used to be agricultural. Now it’s maybe suburban or emerging suburban and— Miroff: Yeah. Rosin: —and still fast evolving, and so there’s a lot of different kinds of people. It’s not just, like, one flat demographic. There’s people of different socioeconomic levels, probably different relationships to Mexico, different relationships to immigration policy, kind of all in this one space. Miroff: Yeah. This is a very kind of aspirational place with a lot of working-class, upwardly mobile families and people who have found jobs in oil and gas, driving to the oil and gas fields. A lot of people have found work in federal law enforcement, working for the Border Patrol, and of course now working for ICE, and also for, you know, cross-border trade. And so this is a place that has for many years really thrived off of its relationship with northern Mexico, with the big assembly plants just south of the border and around the Monterrey, Mexico, region. And so these have been the drivers of the growth for so many years, and these are some of the industries that are also being squeezed by Trump’s presidency. Rosin: Okay. So you get there. You have these thoughts in your head. There’s this very interesting, you know, in the polls, showing this demographic shift, where you’ve got, like, 2016 heavily, heavily Democratic; 2024 goes for Trump. Now the polls are saying: shifting Democratic again. What’s the first thing you see that’s surprising or that catches your eye? Miroff: Well, given how pivotal the Rio Grande Valley is to this election cycle, it’s no surprise that political-advertising money and super-PAC money is just inundating the whole area. And so there are campaign signs lining the highways at all the intersections. And one of the first that caught my eye, actually, was a campaign sign showing this guy Eric Flores. Now, he’s the Republican candidate for the Thirty-Fourth Congressional District, which stretches from Brownsville, kind of hugging the Gulf Coast, all the way up toward Corpus Christi. And most of the campaign signs for Eric Flores just show him with a thumbs-up and his bio. It says he’s an infantry officer, a prosecutor, a father. And they’re very striking ’cause they’re bright red. And then there’s a second set of signs for Flores, and they look just like the first set—they’re also red—but they show him with President Trump. And Trump and Flores are giving the thumbs-up, and it says, across the top of the sign, Trump Endorsed , and below that it says Support ICE . And I saw that sign and I was like, Why would a Republican candidate in the Rio Grande Valley want “Support ICE” on their sign? Well, if you look at the fine print at the bottom of the sign, it says Paid for by Northern Cameron County Democrats . Rosin: Right. Miroff: The Northern Cameron County Democrats are making these signs that show Flores with Trump and that said Support for ICE . [ Music ] Miroff: And so this is a negative sign that the Democrats have put up that just shows the Republican candidate with President Trump on it. And so, you know, that says, I think, everything in this area that voted for Trump two years ago. Running attack ads by just showing the candidate next to the president is, for these Democrats, the most important and effective messaging. Rosin: So what do you read into that strategy? One, you have to distance yourself from Trump, even though he won the election. What else? Like, what else are we learning about ICE or about Trump from a sign like that? Miroff: Well, ICE is overwhelmingly unpopular. It’s no big surprise in an area with a 90 percent Hispanic population. But I think you have to dig a little deeper, and one of the reasons that Trump won in 2024 was his promise to secure the border. This was an area where an overwhelming quantity of migrants arrived under Biden’s presidency. These are some of the communities that were strained the worst by the arrival of hundreds of thousands of people in the first years of Biden’s term. And the perception that he couldn’t really get the situation under control, that the White House wasn’t interested in doing anything about it—these communities were intensely frustrated with that and with the government’s inability to respond, and that was one of the things that helped Trump a lot. But that doesn’t mean that people want ICE officers arresting their friends and family and the ordinary people in their community that don’t have criminal records. And so what I heard over and over again is that, We thought Trump was gonna come for the worst of the worst. We thought he was gonna come in and arrest the criminals. We’re glad that he’s got the border under control, but this is going too far . And so ICE overreach has been a big one there, and then the other thing, which I think is probably the biggest issue for the voters I talked to, is the cost of living and affordability. Rosin: I wanna listen to some of the people that you talked to. One of them was Benny Melendez. Miroff: Do you mind if we switch over to English, Benny? Melendez: No, that’s fine. Let me know. Miroff: For the interview? Cool. Melendez: Yeah, that’s fine. Rosin: Can you talk about that conversation? What did he tell you? Miroff: Yeah, so Benny Melendez is a contractor who asked me to meet him at his job site. And I drove out to this kind of half-built subdivision in the outskirts of McAllen. Miroff: So what are we doing right here, Benny? What is this? Is this a house you’re building? Melendez: Yeah, this is one of my custom homes. Miroff: Okay. Miroff: Benny was there, and he was in this house where his crews had not shown up that day, he said, because word had gone out earlier in the morning that there were ICE officers on patrol in the area, making arrests. Miroff: But there’s nothing happening to this home today? No, you don’t have a crew here? Melendez: No. No, there’s no one here. There’s no—and I called them. I did call them. They told me they were scared, that they were not gonna come today. Miroff: How many guys? Melendez: Mm, let me see. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Miroff: And they saw some ICE vehicles? Or did that, was that on social media, where they— Melendez: Social media, yeah. And the news. They saw it in the morning, so they decided to take the day off. So the ICE agents, they start—if you have a ladder on your truck, they’ll start following you, and they’ll stop you. And if you’re illegal, they’ll arrest you. Miroff: Benny is 32 years old. He grew up in the Rio Grande Valley, and he started his home-building business about seven years ago. And he voted for Trump, and he said he’s just been galvanized by the past two years by ICE arresting—and he said ICE has arrested and deported 15 of the guys that he used to work with. And he said that not only has it made home-building in the Rio Grande Valley much more difficult; it’s really kind of destroying the housing market, he said. It’s the combination of high interest rates, the rise in costs, but also just the inability for homes to get built. He said that he used to be able to get a house built in about four months. Now it takes eight months to a year. [ Music ] Miroff: And so, you know, he said that this has become the issue for him, and he’s gonna do everything he can to get Democrats elected and to send a strong message about the Trump administration going too far in the Rio Grande Valley and arresting people who, you know, in his view, shouldn’t be the target for ICE. Melendez: Yeah, it is difficult for me to hear a 40-, 50-year-old guy cry in private with me, telling me he’s afraid that ICE is gonna take him, ’cause he has to attend this meeting two weeks from now and potentially be deported. Así está pone . That’s how they write it. Potentially be deported. Oh, man, are you gonna be able to sleep in the next two weeks? Rosin: I see why you chose him, ’cause there’s so much in there. Like, he does represent some of the central shifts. I’m curious, you know, when you were talking with him, did you ask him or get the impression that he identifies with either party? Like, does—he thought of himself as a Republican; now he thinks of himself as a Democrat? Or it doesn’t work like that? Like, it’s not about attaching yourself to a party in some way? Miroff: It doesn’t work like that at all, and I think for guys like Benny, there was a certain degree of rebellion in voting for Trump and in bucking, you know, the older generation in the valley that just kind of voted Democrat out of habit. Rosin: Mm-hmm. Miroff: Like many other young men in the valley, I think, and I’m talking about the Rio Grande Valley, there was something a little bit transgressive about voting Republican that signaled that you were an independent thinker. And so he said he’s voting very much against Trump and against the Trump administration and the Republicans this cycle, but he says, you know, very clearly that Democrats are gonna have to earn his support in the future, and that, you know, he’s not taking anything for granted, and he’s gonna vote for whoever he thinks is gonna deliver for the community and is gonna be best for him and his family. Rosin: Yeah. I guess that’s why they’re known as swing voters. That’s literally what they are. Like, they care about a wide range of things, and sometimes those things can be vibes, like, I wanna be transgressive in this election , but sometimes they can be extremely concrete, like, You fired all my workers, and I can’t build homes anymore , you know? Miroff: Yeah. I think one of the takeaways I had from this trip is that even if the Democrats end up doing well in this cycle because there’s so much anger at Trump, it isn’t as if all of these voters are just gonna go back to voting Democrat out of habit, the way they used to. Melendez: Because before voting for Trump, and before voting for the Republicans, I voted for Biden, and I voted for other Democrats, and they have done nothing for my people. Nothing. [ Music ] Miroff: These voters are gonna be up for grabs every single time. Yeah. And they’re gonna go for whichever candidate is really gonna be able to deliver better lives for them and their families. Melendez: What are you gonna do different this time? Are you gonna do the same thing you did when Biden was president? Nothing for my people? I mean, yes, the Republicans, it’s bad with them, but is it better with the Democrats? We’re in a lose-lose situation here. Rosin: After the break, Nick takes us inside a key congressional race in Texas where one Democrat might have a fighting chance against a Republican incumbent in a district that was redrawn by state Republicans. More in a minute. [ Break ] Rosin: Another person you talked to was Bobby Pulido. Who is Bobby Pulido? Miroff: So Bobby Pulido is the Democratic candidate in McAllen area. This is the Fifteenth Congressional District. And Bobby is one of the most fascinating stories of, I think, the entire midterm cycle. And Bobby is a Tejano-music star, and that is a kind of a particular style of South Texas music that is a blend of, kind of, country and pop and, you know, in Spanish. And Bobby had a hit song in the 1990s. He’s a two-time Latin Grammy winner. Rosin: What was the hit song? Just curious. Miroff: It’s called “ Desvelado .” [ “ Desvelado ,” by Bobby Pulido ] Miroff: Which kind of means, like, “sleepless.” It’s about, and the video is really striking. It shows—it was filmed on the streets of San Francisco, and he’s, like, in his early 20s. And he’s kind of going around San Francisco, and he’s thinking about the woman he loves, and he’s just restless. [ “ Desvelado ,” by Bobby Pulido ] Miroff: That song was a huge hit. You know, he was already a star in the Rio Grande Valley before he announced his candidacy, and it’s no wonder that the Democrats recruited him. He comes from a prominent political family down there. And I spent some time driving around the suburbs where he grew up in Edinburg, right outside McAllen. Miroff: So you guys are delivering signs? Campaign staffer: Yep, yep, yep. We try to do this. Obviously we don’t have as much time as we used to. Miroff: And he and his team were delivering yard signs to supporters that had called and, you know, wanted a yard sign. So he was chatting with everybody. He was, you know, knocking on doors and, you know, people were coming out, and they said, Hey, you know, we went to high school together , and, Oh, I remember you , and, Oh, I saw your concert , you know, at so and so. Pulido: Hello. How are y’all doing? Woman: Good. How are you? Miroff: He’s just run this, like, very intensive kind of ground-game strategy to go out and meet as many people as possible. And his opponent, Monica De La Cruz, the incumbent, she got in in 2022, and she made, I think, probably a tactical mistake early on when she kinda tried to dismiss Bobby Pulido as almost like a washed-up quinceañera singer— Rosin: Yeah, yeah. Miroff: —like the guy who plays at the parties for 15-year-old girls. Monica De La Cruz: This election isn’t about who you want performing at your niece’s quinceañera. It’s about who you trust with your family’s future. Miroff: And he took that and he said, Okay, well, I’ll start—if you want me to, just give me a call, and I’ll come and play at your quinceañera . And so he started going around playing for free at all these quinceañera parties. Bobby Pulido: Buenas noches , Alinah. Miroff: He pointed out, you know, he says people are already—they’ve had something to drink, they’re already in a good mood, they’re feeling great, and he gets to, you know, perform and meet hundreds of people. And they see him, and they know he’s running. Pulido: Thank you so much. My name is Bobby Pulido, and I’m running for Congress in District Fifteen. Thank you. Gracias. Rosin: And then what are each of their lines politically? Besides just being fun, like, what is Bobby Pulido’s political line that he’s taking, and then what is Monica De La Cruz’s line in terms of distancing or aligning herself more with Trump? Miroff: Yeah, it’s been very interesting. Pulido has been laser-focused on the affordability issue and ICE overreach. And so he has been the one who, probably more than anyone in the Rio Grande Valley, has highlighted these cases in which, you know, ICE officers have detained U.S. citizens, you know, or outrageous arrests. Pulido: This immigration thing is not just for immigrants. It’s anti-American, because down here, we’ve integrated with them. There’s so many mixed-status families in the Rio Grande Valley—you have no idea. And that’s gonna be the hurricane that’s coming down here, because they’re freaking pissed. Miroff: Pulido’s opponent—the incumbent, Monica De La Cruz—she has, I think, tried to distance herself from Trump’s immigration-enforcement policies. I sat down with her for an interview. Miroff: I wanna start by just asking you, and how much time do you have to answer? Okay. I’ll be pretty succinct. De La Cruz: Sure. Miroff: She said that she believes in a common-sense approach and wants to be kind of a moderate voice. De La Cruz: I have been direct with leadership in saying that enforcement should focus on the criminals and the cartels, not hardworking families that are trying to navigate the complex immigration system. That being said, when I call Washington, D.C., for one of these families, guess what? They pick up the phone, and they answer my calls, and we look for real solutions, not only in immigration. Miroff: But she, as did all the other Republicans, voted for two funding packages that have given the Department of Homeland Security nearly a quarter of a trillion dollars for immigration enforcement. And that includes more than $100 billion for ICE, more than 10 times its annual budget. And so she’s tried to kind of distance herself from Trump’s immigration-enforcement policies and highlight some kind of the affordability messaging that she thinks is gonna be a winner, like around her support for the no tax on tips. De La Cruz: No tax on tips, no tax on Social Security, no tax on overtime. Miroff: But, you know, in her campaign literature, she doesn’t, like, you know, appear alongside the president. And so she’s one of the Republicans that’s also, I think, trying to put some distance between her and the White House. Miroff: I’m down with what—I mean, there’s a dog on the porch. Roel Garza: Oh, yeah. Okay. Miroff: But he’s not barking at us. Rosin: You also went door-knocking with a canvasser for Democrats. Did you learn anything from talking to voters that way? Miroff: I did. You know, it was really fascinating. This was a young man, a 20-year-old student named Roel Garza. Miroff: Are you a college student, or are you older? Garza: I just graduated. I’m 20. I just graduated from college, but I’m doing my master’s now, my M.B.A. Miroff: You know, he had the addresses of people who had voted in the last election and, you know, he had an interesting strategy. He would go and knock on their door and ask them, What are the issues that you care about? What are the problems in your community that you wanna see fixed? He would take their answers, and then he would try to describe the solutions that Democratic candidates were proposing for some of the things that mattered to them, as a way to kinda steer them to the candidates, you know, before he would hand them some campaign literature endorsing very much the Democratic ticket. Garza: And you could go vote at any polling location in Hidalgo County. Woman: Okay. Garza: So these are the candidates that we’re endorsing—James Talarico, Bobby Pulido—and in the back you have some more. Miroff: It was really eye-opening. It was a good reminder that a lot of people who are busy, who have busy lives, are not paying that much attention, not as much attention to politics as, you know, reporters and candidates. And it was also interesting to hear from working-class folks who voted for Trump last time, you know? I think one of the things that struck me the most was that there’s still a degree of kind of sympathy for Trump himself, that people think they sort of see him as this kind of outside figure who has shaken things up. And I was also struck by the degree to which they were kind of confused about the candidates, and they had seen so much negative advertising that they really didn’t know what to believe. [ Music ] Miroff: And so I think there’s a lot of confusion. I think there’s a high probability that a lot of these people are just gonna end up splitting their tickets and are gonna vote for candidates with whom they think they can be comfortable with regardless of their party affiliation. Rosin: So what we know about the pattern is: In 2024, as we discussed, Trump won a more diverse coalition than anyone expected. Then Democrats had their reckoning. It sounds like that’s all playing out in the places where you visited. If there was a swing back to Democrats now, what do you think would be the correct thing to understand about it, and what would be a misunderstanding about it? Miroff: Well, I do think the two most salient issues are the cost of living. You know, think about how many Hispanic families in the United States are blue-collar, who aspire to, you know, joining the middle class. And so if they’re getting squeezed, I think that that is really gonna hurt, you know, whichever candidate is gonna take the blame for that or gonna be associated with that. But then the big one also is overreach on immigration enforcement. And again, you know, people voted for border security. Border security is broadly popular in the United States. People do not like images of chaos and disorder along the border, but that doesn’t mean that they want intense ICE enforcement on the streets. And, you know, what they see on the streets of, you know, U.S. cities with ICE arrests also looks chaotic and ugly. And whenever people see what immigration enforcement looks like, they often kind of recoil from it. And so for Hispanic families who feel like they’re being targeted, and that the people who are backing the president who are his core supporters are speaking in just openly racist terms, it once more, I think, questions for them whether the Republican Party wants them in the United States. Rosin: Yeah. Miroff: I mean, if you’re a minority in this country and one of the parties is speaking in a way that makes you feel like they consider you less American and even less human, then why would you vote for them? You know, to the extent that these are kind of unresolved tensions within the Republican Party—I’m wondering if this midterm result, especially if there’s a blue wave and it’s driven partly by Hispanic voters—if this forces some kind of reckoning within the Republican Party about whether or not you really want racists openly part of your coalition if it’s gonna drive away so many other voters. Rosin: Well, Nick, thank you again for joining us. Miroff: Oh, my pleasure. Anytime. [ Music ] Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Jinae West with help from Rosie Hughes. It was edited by Kevin Townsend. Fact-checking by Gisela Salim-Peyer and Sam Fentress. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. And in case you haven’t heard, this Tuesday night, November 3, we’re going to host a special Election Night livestream. I’ll be joined by my Radio Atlantic co-host, Adam Harris. We’ll talk with Atlantic staffers about midterm results as they come in and what new directions the country could be headed in. We’ll have familiar guests like Tom Nichols, David Frum, and Anne Applebaum, among others. We’ll be live for two hours starting at 9 p.m. eastern. And, as always, listeners, if you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener . I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.

items.title: Breast Cancer: Breast Society leads awareness walk to promote early detection
items.description: The Breast Society of Ghana has intensified efforts to promote breast cancer awareness and early detection following an awareness walk through parts of Accra’s central business district on Saturday, October 24, 2026. Held under the theme “Early Action, Better Outcomes,” the walk aimed to encourage early breast cancer screening and educate the public on the importance of taking proactive steps to protect their breast health. The event began at 6:30 a.m. with an aerobics session at Independence Square before participants proceeded through the busy Makola Market area, engaging traders, customers and other members of the public along the route. At Makola Market and Kinbu, medical personnel and breast cancer survivors led interactive educational sessions in various local languages, making information about breast cancer more accessible to people in the communities. The discussions focused on breast cancer screening guidelines and the importance of screening before symptoms develop, while participants distributed educational leaflets to traders, shoppers and passersby in Accra’s central business district. The President of the Breast Society of Ghana underscored the importance of breast screening, noting that early detection and prompt treatment significantly improve outcomes for people diagnosed with breast cancer. The event was also attended by the Society’s Founder, Professor Clegg-Lamptey, whose longstanding commitment to breast cancer awareness and care continues to inspire efforts to combat the disease in Ghana. Security Agencies, Corporate Bodies Join Campaign The awareness walk attracted participants from various institutions, including the Ghana Armed Forces, Ghana National Fire Service, Ghana Immigration Service, Ghana Police Service and Ghana Prisons Service. Corporate organisations, community groups, professional societies and individuals also joined the exercise, demonstrating broad support for efforts to improve breast cancer awareness and encourage preventive health practices. Their participation highlighted the importance of collective action in reaching more people with information about breast cancer and the benefits of early screening. Partners Support Breast Health Education The initiative was organised in collaboration with Jhpiego, the Ghana Health Service (GHS) and the Ministry of Health. The partnership strengthened the event’s public education efforts, enabling organisers to engage communities directly and share information on breast cancer screening and early intervention. Sulu Investments, makers of Nero Prime water, supported the exercise by providing drinking water throughout the walk to keep participants hydrated. Renewed Commitment to Early Detection The Breast Society of Ghana’s awareness walk formed part of broader efforts to promote breast health education and encourage people to take screening seriously. By taking the campaign directly to busy commercial areas, the Society sought to reach people who might otherwise have limited opportunities to participate in formal health education programmes. The event also provided a platform for breast cancer survivors and medical professionals to engage the public, share knowledge and reinforce the importance of early action. The Society reaffirmed its commitment to sustained breast cancer education and awareness initiatives, emphasising the need for continued public engagement to encourage early detection and improve outcomes.

items.title: Foncier : Mettre fin au désordre
items.description: © Internet La dissolution du Conseil communal de la Commune I remet une vieille plaie au centre de l’actualité : le foncier. Morcellements irréguliers, reconnaissances contestées de droits, documents délivrés en dehors des règles, chevauchements de titres… Les griefs reviennent avec une constance inquiétante. Le problème dépasse pourtant cette seule mairie. Depuis des années, le foncier figure parmi les principales sources de réclamations adressées au Médiateur de la République. Il mobilise maires, services des Domaines, autorités administratives, tribunaux et citoyens, souvent au terme de procédures longues, coûteuses et éprouvantes. Les textes existent pourtant. Les compétences des collectivités sont encadrées, le Titre foncier demeure la référence en matière de propriété et les abus peuvent être sanctionnés. Le Mali vient même de franchir une nouvelle étape avec la mise en place d’un Pôle spécialisé en matière foncière, conçu pour mieux traiter des contentieux dispersés entre plusieurs juridictions. Il faudra maintenant que cet outil fasse la différence sur le terrain. Car le vrai problème n’est plus seulement l’absence de règles. C’est leur application, leur respect par les administrations concernées et la capacité de la justice à trancher au plus vite. Le citoyen qui achète une parcelle ne devrait pas découvrir des années plus tard qu’elle a été attribuée deux fois, qu’elle empiète sur un domaine public ou que le document qui lui a été remis n’a pas la valeur qu’il croyait. Mettre fin au désordre foncier, c’est d’abord rendre la règle claire, la décision traçable et la responsabilité effective. À ce prix, la confiance pourra revenir dans un secteur où trop de familles ont tout perdu.

items.title: Two dead in rock spire collapse at tourist site in Turkiye's Cappadocia
items.description: A landslide triggered by heavy rainfall caused a rock spire to collapse in Turkey’s Cappadocia tourist region on Thursday, killing two people, the local governor said. “We have recovered the bodies of two people who lost their lives. One injured person was taken to hospital,” Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok said. The incident occurred at 3:15pm local time (5:15pm PKT) when a landslide triggered a rockfall in the town of Goreme near the open-air museum, Kok said. The area was closed to the public following the collapse, according to reports Eyewitnesses reported hearing a loud noise as the rock spire fell. “Our search and rescue operations at the scene are ongoing. The government is continuing its efforts at the scene with all available resources,” Kok said. Turkiye’s Cappadocia region, a magnet for tourists from around the world, is home to rock formations known as “fairy chimneys”, created by ancient volcanic activity.

items.title: Reps seek review of NCC phone rules over price hike fears
items.description: By Gift Chapi Odekina, Abuja The House of Representatives has called for a review of the Nigerian Communications Commission’s (NCC) mobile device verification requirements over concerns that the policy could increase phone prices and lead to the wrongful blocking of legitimate used devices. The House warned that additional compliance costs under the framework could increase expenses for phone importers and retailers, with consumers, particularly low-income Nigerians, likely to bear the burden through higher prices. The resolution followed a motion sponsored by a Kano lawmaker, Sani Wakili, urging the commission to review the implementation of its device verification framework in consultation with relevant stakeholders. The framework, operated through the Device Management System and the Central Equipment Identity Register, enables the identification and verification of mobile phones and other SIM-enabled devices using their International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) numbers. Lawmakers noted that the enhanced verification requirements, which took effect on October 7, 2026, impose additional compliance obligations on newly imported devices, potentially raising operating costs for importers and retailers. They expressed concern that businesses could transfer the additional expenses to consumers, making mobile phones less affordable for Nigerians who rely on them for communication, education, banking and other commercial activities. The House also raised concerns about possible technical errors, database mismatches and limitations in the commission’s scanning and verification systems, warning that such challenges could result in legitimate devices being wrongly rejected or blocked. According to the lawmakers, the second-hand phone market could be particularly affected, given that used devices offer a more affordable alternative to new phones for many Nigerians. While acknowledging the NCC’s efforts to tackle counterfeit, cloned and stolen mobile phones, the House stressed that enforcement should not unfairly penalise legitimate businesses or restrict access to affordable communication devices. Consequently, the lawmakers urged the commission to review the framework’s implementation, simplify verification procedures and reduce compliance costs. They also called for a fair and accessible verification process for used and second-hand mobile phones to prevent legitimate devices from being wrongly flagged or blocked. To further examine the concerns, the House mandated its Committees on Communications and Commerce to engage the NCC and other relevant stakeholders on the implementation of the requirements and report back within four weeks for further legislative action. The Committee on Legislative Compliance was also directed to ensure compliance with the resolution. The proposed review comes amid growing reliance on mobile phones for essential economic and social activities, including digital financial services, online learning, electronic commerce and communication. For many Nigerians, second-hand devices remain the most affordable option. A verification system that wrongly excludes legitimate used phones could therefore affect consumers as well as small-scale traders whose livelihoods depend on buying and reselling the devices. The House’s intervention seeks to ensure that the NCC’s efforts to strengthen device security do not inadvertently increase costs for consumers or create unnecessary difficulties for legitimate businesses. The outcome of the proposed engagement is expected to help determine whether the framework’s current implementation adequately balances device security, regulatory compliance, consumer protection and affordability. items.title: Sam George confirmed as chair of AU communication and ICT committee
items.description: Ghana’s Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, has been confirmed as Chair of the African Union Specialised Technical Committee on Communication and ICT (AU STC-ICT) for a two-year term. His confirmation took place at the committee’s 6th Ordinary Session in Libreville, Gabon, where he called on African countries to move beyond policy declarations and accelerate the implementation of digital transformation initiatives. Mr George described the chairmanship as a responsibility to the entire African Union, stressing the need for stronger continental cooperation to advance Africa’s digital ambitions. “I accept such responsibility not as a privilege for one country, but as a duty to our entire union,” he said in his opening address to the ministerial session. Mr George said Africa had developed important policy frameworks covering digital transformation, artificial intelligence and data governance but had struggled to implement them at the pace required. “What we have too often lacked is the collective will to implement them at the pace that our people demand,” he stated. He identified connectivity, data governance, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence as priority areas requiring coordinated action by member states. The minister also urged African countries to strengthen their collective bargaining power in the global digital economy, arguing that a unified approach would give the continent greater influence in negotiations on technology, data and digital trade. “When we negotiate alone, we are 55 separate markets, but when we negotiate together, we are a market of nearly 1.5 billion people,” he said. He added that Africa must be “at the table, not on the menu” in global discussions on artificial intelligence, data and digital trade. Mr George also emphasised the need to equip Africa’s young population with the skills and opportunities to participate in the digital economy. He cited Ghana’s One Million Coders Programme as an example of efforts to provide young people with the tools to innovate and contribute to technological development. He said Africa’s digital transformation would depend not only on policy frameworks and infrastructure but also on the ability of its people to develop solutions and create economic opportunities. Setting out his priorities for the chairmanship, Mr George pledged to build consensus among member states, strengthen cooperation and promote the implementation of agreed digital initiatives. “Over the next two years, this committee must be measured not by the declarations that we adopt, but by the results that we deliver,” he said. He called on member states to take decisive action towards a shared digital future in which African countries could operate as one digital market and speak with a stronger collective voice. Ghana’s chairmanship comes as countries across the continent seek to expand digital connectivity, strengthen cybersecurity, advance responsible artificial intelligence development and improve their participation in the global digital economy.

items.title: Emprunt obligataire 2026 : 4 579 milliards GNF mobilisés, Mariama Ciré Sylla salue la performance du secteur bancaire guinéen
items.description: Au terme de l’emprunt obligataire 2026, l’État guinéen a mobilisé 4 579,145 milliards de francs guinéens, dépassant largement son objectif initial de 2 500 milliards GNF. Pour saluer cette performance, le ministère de l’Économie, des Finances et du Budget a organisé, ce jeudi 29 octobre 2026, un déjeuner de remerciement en l’honneur des établissements bancaires ayant contribué à la réussite de cette opération. La rencontre a réuni la ministre Mariama Ciré Sylla, le gouverneur de la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée (BCRG), Karamo Kaba, ainsi que les responsables des institutions financières partenaires. C’est une mobilisation qui dépasse les attentes initiales du gouvernement. Lancé avec un objectif de 2 500 milliards de francs guinéens, l’emprunt obligataire 2026 a enregistré des souscriptions de 4 579,145 milliards GNF, soit un taux de couverture de 183,17 %. Un résultat qui témoigne, selon les responsables présents, du potentiel de l’épargne nationale et de la capacité du marché financier guinéen à contribuer au financement des politiques publiques. À l’occasion de ce déjeuner de remerciement, les autorités ont salué l’engagement des établissements bancaires, tout en soulignant la nécessité de transformer cette mobilisation financière en investissements concrets au bénéfice des populations. Laurent Fondjo salue une démonstration de la capacité financière de la Guinée Prenant la parole au nom du syndicat de placement, Laurent Fondjo, administrateur général et directeur général d’Afriland First Bank Guinée, chef de file et arrangeur de l’opération, s’est réjoui de l’issue de cette mobilisation, qu’il a présentée comme une démonstration de la capacité du pays à mobiliser ses ressources internes. Revenant sur les interrogations qui avaient accompagné le lancement de l’emprunt, il a rappelé les défis auxquels les acteurs financiers étaient confrontés pour convaincre les Guinéens de souscrire à cette opération. « Plus tard, Mme la ministre, sous votre leadership, nous avons convié ici, nous nous sommes retrouvés ici avec les membres du syndicat et les principaux acteurs du système financier et vous nous avez une fois de plus demandé de “mouiller le maillot”, comme on dit dans le langage du football. Nous vous avons promis que cela sera fait et que cela sera bien fait », a-t-il déclaré. Pour lui, les résultats obtenus traduisent la confiance des investisseurs locaux dans les perspectives économiques du pays. « La Guinée montre aux yeux du monde qu'elle est capable de lever les ressources domestiques. Et parfois, les gens ne font pas le lien avec les ressources étrangères », a-t-il souligné. Laurent Fondjo a notamment comparé les ressources mobilisées sur le marché national au financement évoqué dans le cadre du programme conclu avec le Fonds monétaire international (FMI). « Mme la ministre, vous avez signé un programme avec le FMI, c'est autour de 430 millions de dollars. Aujourd'hui, en Guinée, nous avons levé 520 millions de dollars. Donc, nous avons fait plus que le FMI », a-t-il affirmé. Il a également insisté sur la disponibilité des ressources mobilisées, destinées notamment au financement des infrastructures et des projets de développement. « Notre argent est disponible, c'est dans le compte du Trésor. Monsieur le gouverneur peut confirmer que l'argent est disponible et prêt pour financer nos infrastructures, prêt pour financer notre développement », a-t-il ajouté. Le responsable d’Afriland First Bank Guinée a par ailleurs révélé que des citoyens continuaient à manifester leur intérêt pour l’opération, même après la clôture des souscriptions. « Cette semaine, plein de Guinéens sont venus vers moi pour dire : “Mais nous voulons encore souscrire à l’emprunt.” Je leur ai dit : “Mais il y avait un délai, le délai est passé.” Je leur ai dit : “S'il vous plaît, demandez à l'État de lancer encore notre emprunt parce que nous voyons que les choses avancent” », a-t-il rapporté. Selon lui, cette réaction illustre l’impact de l’opération sur la perception des citoyens et la confiance qu’elle contribue à renforcer entre les acteurs économiques et les institutions publiques. Sept établissements mobilisés pour dépasser l’objectif initial Présentant les résultats détaillés de l’opération, Laurent Fondjo a indiqué que les sept établissements bancaires du syndicat de placement avaient contribué à la mobilisation des ressources. Afriland First Bank Guinée arrive en tête avec 1 366,650 milliards GNF, soit environ 29,85 % des souscriptions. Vista Banque Guinée a mobilisé 670,980 milliards GNF, représentant 14,65 % du total, tandis que la Banque pour le commerce et l’industrie (BCI) a contribué à hauteur de 664,700 milliards GNF, soit 14,52 %. Ecobank a mobilisé 626,315 milliards GNF, correspondant à 13,68 % des souscriptions. OraBank Guinée a apporté 500,500 milliards GNF, soit 10,93 %, tandis que Sky Bank a contribué à hauteur de 400 milliards GNF, soit 8,74 %. AFG Banque Guinée a, pour sa part, mobilisé 350 milliards GNF, représentant 7,64 % du montant total. Au total, l’opération a permis de mobiliser des ressources correspondant à 915 829 000 obligations, selon les chiffres communiqués par le chef de file. À l’issue de son intervention, Laurent Fondjo a remercié le ministère de l’Économie, des Finances et du Budget, la Banque centrale, la Direction générale des Financements, ainsi que les équipes techniques et de communication ayant participé à la réussite de l’opération. Karamo Kaba plaide pour un marché financier plus ouvert et des échéances plus longues Pour le gouverneur de la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée, Karamo Kaba, le montant mobilisé, le taux d’intérêt et la durée de remboursement constituent des indicateurs essentiels pour apprécier la confiance des investisseurs envers un pays. Illustrant son propos, il a rappelé qu’au-delà des discours et des promesses, le marché financier exprime concrètement son appréciation à travers les conditions auxquelles il accepte de financer un État. « Le conseiller lui répond en fait, par le montant qu'il accepte de nous prêter. Par le taux d'intérêt auquel il accepte de nous prêter. Et par la durée qu'il nous prête », a-t-il expliqué. Le gouverneur a salué le taux de couverture de 183,17 %, qu’il a qualifié d’extraordinaire, tout en félicitant les établissements bancaires et les souscripteurs guinéens pour leur participation. Il a également mis en avant les conditions de l’émission, notamment un taux d’intérêt annuel de 11 % pour une maturité de cinq ans. « Aujourd'hui, 11 % avec un taux d'inflation à 6 %, c'est quelque chose qui est plutôt bien. Et les Guinéens sont déjà rationnels. C'est un très bon placement », a-t-il estimé. Karamo Kaba a par ailleurs encouragé les autorités à envisager des échéances plus longues pour les prochaines émissions, soulignant que la forte demande enregistrée pourrait permettre d’explorer de nouvelles possibilités de financement. « Mon conseil, c'est vraiment d'allonger de plus en plus la maturité. Parce que si c'est sursouscrit, c'est qu'il y a des gens qui veulent prendre du risque. C'est qu'il y a des gens qui veulent s'engager », a-t-il déclaré. Le gouverneur a enfin plaidé pour un élargissement de la participation aux prochaines opérations, afin de ne pas limiter la mobilisation des ressources au seul secteur bancaire. « Ce qu'on devrait faire, c'est voir comment les assureurs aussi peuvent participer. Voir comment les institutions de microfinance peuvent nous accompagner », a-t-il recommandé. Cette diversification des souscripteurs permettrait, selon cette orientation, d’approfondir le marché financier national et d’accroître les capacités de financement de l’économie guinéenne. Aboubacar Sidiki Diakité qualifie les résultats d’exceptionnels Pour sa part, le directeur général des Financements, Aboubacar Sidiki Diakité, a salué les résultats de cette opération, mettant l’accent sur l’écart significatif entre le montant initialement recherché et les ressources effectivement mobilisées. « L'objectif initial qui a été recherché, c'était 2 500 milliards de francs. Nous avons fini à 4 579 milliards. Ce qui est, en réalité, un résultat exceptionnel », a-t-il déclaré. Sans revenir longuement sur les chiffres déjà présentés, il a souligné la portée des résultats obtenus, qui constituent, selon lui, un signal important pour le financement de l’économie nationale. Cette performance vient renforcer les perspectives de mobilisation de ressources sur le marché intérieur, dans un contexte où les autorités cherchent à diversifier les sources de financement des projets publics. Mariama Ciré Sylla appelle à transformer la confiance en résultats concrets Clôturant les interventions, la ministre de l’Économie, des Finances et du Budget, Mariama Ciré Sylla, a exprimé sa reconnaissance aux établissements bancaires, à la Banque centrale et aux équipes techniques ayant contribué à la réussite de l’emprunt obligataire. Elle a salué une mobilisation qu’elle considère comme un signal positif envoyé aux acteurs économiques nationaux et aux partenaires internationaux. « Grâce à votre mobilisation, on a pu atteindre 4 579 milliards de nos francs. Donc, c'est une réussite, c'est un succès remarquable. Dans un environnement incertain, vous avez choisi de faire confiance en la Guinée, en sa stabilité, en ses perspectives économiques, mais aussi en sa capacité d'honorer ses engagements. Je mesure l'importance de cette confiance », a-t-elle déclaré. La ministre a particulièrement salué la contribution d’Afriland First Bank Guinée, chef de file de l’opération, avant de remercier individuellement les autres établissements pour leur participation. Elle a également insisté sur la nécessité de préserver cette confiance dans la durée, en rappelant que la crédibilité financière d’un État se construit à travers ses actes et le respect de ses engagements. « La confiance ne se décrète pas. Elle se mérite par les actes. Et on va travailler dans la transparence et dans le respect de nos obligations à nous assurer qu'elle se consolide pour que l'année prochaine on ait un succès encore plus éclatant », a-t-elle affirmé. Pour Mariama Ciré Sylla, cette opération met en évidence trois enseignements majeurs. Le premier concerne la crédibilité financière de la Guinée et la confiance accordée à sa signature souveraine. Le deuxième porte sur la capacité du pays à mobiliser l’épargne nationale pour soutenir son développement. Le troisième renvoie à la responsabilité des autorités dans l’utilisation efficace et transparente des ressources obtenues. Sur ce dernier point, la ministre a souligné que la réussite d’un emprunt ne se mesure pas uniquement aux montants collectés, mais également aux retombées concrètes des investissements réalisés. « Notre responsabilité, c'est de nous assurer que ces fonds seront utilisés avec efficacité, transparence et que chaque investissement produise une véritable valeur ajoutée pour l'économie nationale », a-t-elle insisté. Elle a notamment évoqué le financement de projets structurants dans les secteurs de l’éducation, de la santé et de l’énergie, considérés comme essentiels à l’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations. La ministre a également réaffirmé la volonté du gouvernement de renforcer le partenariat avec les établissements bancaires, au-delà de cette opération, à travers un dialogue permanent fondé sur la confiance, la transparence et une vision commune du développement économique. Au-delà des résultats immédiats, la réussite de l’emprunt obligataire 2026 ouvre des perspectives pour le développement du marché financier national. Les interventions ont notamment mis en évidence la nécessité d’élargir la base des investisseurs, d’encourager une participation accrue des compagnies d’assurance et des institutions de microfinance, et d’explorer des échéances de remboursement plus longues. Youssouf Keita L’article Emprunt obligataire 2026 : 4 579 milliards GNF mobilisés, Mariama Ciré Sylla salue la performance du secteur bancaire guinéen est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Seidu Agongo tells youth to match talent with hard work as 10,000 sewing machine drive begins
items.description: Businessman and philanthropist Alhaji Seidu Agongo has urged young Ghanaians to believe in their talents and pursue them with determination, saying emerging from humble backgrounds to success is not a fantasy but an achievable reality for those willing to work for it. Speaking on Wednesday after the presentation of the first batch of free sewing machines under his nationwide initiative to distribute 10,000 machines to vulnerable women and youth, Agongo said Ghana was blessed with talented young people whose potential could be unlocked with the right support. “You should not be shy about your talents, no. Once it is a genuine talent, pursue it and commit your energy, your heart and your time to them,” he said. “Breakthroughs are not miracles you only see in movies or read about in books. They are real, but they must be backed by hard work, commitment and a goal.” According to him, many young Ghanaians possess the skills and creativity needed to compete on the global stage, but often lack the opportunities and resources to develop their abilities. This, he said informed his decision to always offer support whenever possible, with the hope that beneficiaries will capitalise on the opportunities to improve upon their lives. Partnership with NEIP Agongo is implementing the initiative in partnership with the National Entrepreneurship and Innovation Programme (NEIP) to empower women and young people with employable skills and provide them with tools needed to start or expand tailoring and dressmaking businesses. More than 800 units were distributed during the first phase with others planned for later dates. Interested persons have to fill a form available on Seidu Agongo’s social media platforms to stand the chance of qualifying for a free machine. Agongo said the programme was also a reflection of his belief in sharing opportunities and supporting vulnerable members of society. The founder of the collapsed Heritage Bank Limited told beneficiaries to make good use of the machines to improve their lives and create opportunities for others around them. “We all need kindness. Whatever your situation, I will say don’t despair. I want to help everyone as much as possible. I want to live by people’s happiness,” he said. “There is room for everyone if we genuinely support each other. I have always believed in sharing, supporting and being there for everyone whenever I can.” He described the initiative as a continuation of his long-held belief in giving back to society and helping others become self-reliant. He further expressed the hope that beneficiaries will put the machines to proper use, gain from them and use the little they get to advance their lives and the lives of those around them. “At the end, we will be better and God and Ghana will be the winner,” he added. Other initiatives The sewing machines donation is the latest in a series of interventions by Agongo aimed at supporting young people, women and vulnerable groups. Over the years, the businessman has supported skills training, educational programmes, entrepreneurship initiatives and humanitarian causes through various personal and corporate interventions. Beneficiaries at the event welcomed the donation, saying it would help them establish small businesses, earn sustainable incomes and reduce their dependence on others. The nationwide distribution exercise is expected to continue in phases until all 10,000 sewing machines have been handed over to beneficiaries across the country.

items.title: La bouteille à la mer numérique (Par Samboudian KAMARA)
items.description: À l'heure où les institutions rivalisent de modernité numérique, certaines semblent avoir trouvé dans WhatsApp le substitut idéal aux circuits officiels de communication. L’un des effets de la révolution numérique dans la presse est que le communiqué affecté à un relais bien identifié a cédé la place à un texte « balancé » dans les groupes. Alors que les outils digitaux de l’ère moderne sont censés alléger la charge de travail des journalistes, ces derniers se voient obligés, s’ils entendent rester dans les canons de leur métier, d’opérer une double vérification : n’y a-t-il pas usurpation de l’identité de la personne ou de l’organisation qui adresse le message ? Cette première question résolue, il leur faut attester que le message lui-même est véridique ? Combien de fois le tampon « fake news » a été apposé sur un document après le constat d’un logo déformé, d’un en-tête bizarre, d’une typographie incohérente, d’une date suspecte, de mentions administratives manquantes ? Et le must, les fautes de grammaire et/ou d’orthographe… Jeter la proie pour l’ombre : ainsi peut être décrite la nouvelle faiblesse observée depuis quelques mois dans la communication institutionnelle de plusieurs organisations. Suivant le nouveau paradigme faisant des réseaux sociaux la voie indiquée pour communiquer efficacement, les déplacements des autorités, les décisions ministérielles, l’agenda de certains programmes, voire les textes de loi, l’essentiel passe maintenant par WhatsApp. Pour une décision de justice rendue en mai 2025 dans le cadre du recours d’un fonctionnaire devant la Cour suprême contre son limogeage par le ministre de la Santé, ce n’est que le mercredi 6 août suivant, soit trois mois après le verdict, que l’arrêt est apparu comme par enchantement dans des groupes WhatsApp. Le lendemain, au moins cinq quotidiens y consacraient leur « Une ». C’est l’exemple le moins frappant, car régulièrement, la com’ relative aux voyages des autorités, à certaines décisions ministérielles, à des événements officiels, à des questions de la plus haute importance, est « gérée » sous la forme de partage dans des groupes certes touchant un grand nombre, mais ouverts aux vents de la désinformation et de la manipulation. C’est une démarche « tendance », bien à propos dans un contexte de démantèlement des canaux institutionnels d’échanges au profit du numérique. Une idée du reste largement partagée maintenant veut que « la presse », en tant qu’institution, ne soit plus le cadre pertinent pour communiquer. Une tendance renforcée à la faveur de l’alternance politique en avril 2024 avec une nouvelle majorité portée par le postulat que Facebook, TikTok, YouTube ont été leurs principaux facteurs de mobilisation, selon le nouveau mantra, ce qui est vrai. La situation est fort désagréable pour certains éditeurs de presse qui se voient ainsi obligés de mettre sur la balance ce qui fonde, si elle n’est pas dévoyée, leur valeur professionnelle : la sélection, la vérification, le recoupement, le traitement spécifique suivant un angle. Si le journalisme est considéré comme une forme de production de connaissances valides, c’est parce qu’un cadre normatif en valide les étapes : collecte-recoupement – vérification (si possible triangulation) – mise en forme – présentation. Ce que ne permettent pas les réseaux sociaux. Auparavant, existait un agenda. Les heures précédant un événement, les rédactions recevaient des invitations et/ou des communiqués de presse, programmaient ensuite leur couverture selon un format qui permettait d’identifier toutes les parties prenantes au processus, en plus de la disponibilité d’interlocuteurs officiels. Or, les réseaux sociaux, s’ils n’ont pas leur pareil pour toucher le plus grand nombre, n’en restent pas moins ouverts aux fausses informations, à la manipulation, à l’anonymat de la source. Ce qui est aux antipodes des valeurs journalistiques, celles qui exigent la diffusion d’une information complète et porteuse de sens. Naturellement, un retour en arrière n’est pas envisageable. Le public lit moins, les médias traversent une crise de confiance vis-à-vis de leur lectorat, la possibilité d’être informé via le téléphone portable transforme les réceptions. À cet égard, les organisations gagneraient à réhabiliter les canaux qui garantissent la traçabilité et l'identification de l'émetteur : listes de diffusion par courrier électronique (mailing), communiqués transmis aux rédactions et aux agences de presse, espaces de presse sur les sites institutionnels régulièrement mis à jour. À l’heure où la désinformation prospère sur la confusion des sources, communiquer vite ne suffit plus, il faut aussi viser juste. samboudian.kamara@lesoleil.sn

items.title: Interview : « Une mauvaise conservation des aliments ou une manipulation inappropriée peuvent provoquer des intoxications alimentaires » (Anselme Bruno Sandah)
items.description: La qualité et la sécurité des repas servis dans les restaurants suscitent parfois des interrogations chez les consommateurs. Entre les conditions de conservation des aliments, le respect des règles d’hygiène et la fraîcheur des ingrédients utilisés, certains clients s’interrogent sur les risques que peuvent présenter les mets préparés hors de leur domicile. Comment les chefs cuisiniers préviennent-ils ces risques ? Quelles garanties peuvent-ils apporter aux consommateurs ? Dans cette interview, M. Anselme Bruno Sandah, secrétaire général adjoint de l’Union des chefs cuisiniers du Togo (UCCT), revient sur les exigences et les responsabilités des professionnels de la restauration. ATOP : Certains consommateurs doutent de la qualité sanitaire des repas servis dans les restaurants. Ces inquiétudes sont-elles justifiées ? Anselme Bruno Sandah : Les consommateurs ont raison d’accorder une attention particulière à ce qu’ils mangent. La sécurité alimentaire est une responsabilité importante pour tous les professionnels de la restauration. Un repas ne doit pas seulement être bon au goût ou bien présenté. Il doit également être préparé dans des conditions qui préservent la santé du consommateur. Une mauvaise conservation des aliments, un défaut d’hygiène ou une manipulation inappropriée peuvent favoriser la contamination des produits et provoquer des intoxications alimentaires. C’est pourquoi le chef cuisinier doit rester vigilant à toutes les étapes, depuis le choix des ingrédients jusqu’au service. ATOP : Concrètement, comment un chef cuisinier peut-il garantir la qualité des mets proposés à ses clients ? M. Sandah : Cela commence par le choix des produits. Le chef doit vérifier leur fraîcheur, leur état et leur provenance autant que possible. Il doit ensuite respecter les conditions de conservation adaptées à chaque aliment. La viande, le poisson, les produits laitiers et les plats préparés, par exemple, nécessitent une attention particulière en matière de température et de durée de conservation. Les denrées doivent être stockées dans des conditions appropriées et les produits altérés ne doivent pas être utilisés. Il faut également respecter les règles de préparation et de cuisson, nettoyer les équipements et veiller à la propreté de l’espace de travail. La sécurité d’un repas repose sur l’ensemble de ces précautions. ATOP : Certains établissements rencontrent des difficultés liées au manque d’équipements de réfrigération. Es-ce un risque supplémentaire ? M. Sandah : Le manque d’équipements adaptés peut effectivement compliquer la conservation des produits périssables. Les réfrigérateurs et les chambres froides, lorsqu’ils sont nécessaires, contribuent à maintenir les aliments dans de bonnes conditions. Lorsqu’un établissement ne dispose pas des équipements appropriés, il doit redoubler de vigilance dans la gestion de ses approvisionnements et de ses stocks. Mais il faut être clair, les contraintes matérielles ne doivent pas conduire à négliger la sécurité des consommateurs. Les professionnels doivent prendre toutes les précautions possibles et ne pas servir des aliments dont la qualité sanitaire est douteuse. ATOP : Au-delà de la conservation, quelles sont les principales précautions à prendre dans une cuisine pour éviter les contaminations ? M. Sandah : L’hygiène est indispensable. Les mains doivent être lavées régulièrement, les plans de travail et les ustensiles nettoyés correctement. Il faut aussi éviter les contacts entre les aliments crus et les aliments prêts à être consommés. Les ustensiles utilisés pour manipuler les viandes, les volailles, les poissons et les légumes doivent être gérés de manière à limiter les contaminations croisées. La cuisson doit également être adaptée aux aliments préparés. Enfin, le chef a la responsabilité d’organiser le travail de son équipe et de veiller à ce que chaque membre respecte les consignes. La sécurité alimentaire est un effort collectif qui exige de la discipline au quotidien. ATOP : Comment les consommateurs peuvent-ils savoir si un restaurant accorde réellement de l’importance à ces exigences ? M. Sandah : La propreté générale des lieux, l’entretien des équipements et les conditions dans lesquelles les aliments sont manipulés peuvent donner des indications aux clients. Toutefois, l’apparence d’un établissement ou d’un plat ne suffit pas, à elle seule, à garantir sa sécurité sanitaire. C’est pourquoi les professionnels doivent faire preuve de transparence, de rigueur et de responsabilité. Les contrôles sanitaires et la sensibilisation des acteurs de la restauration sont également importants. Notre objectif doit être de gagner et de préserver la confiance des consommateurs grâce à des pratiques responsables. ATOP : Les chefs cuisiniers ont-ils également un rôle à jouer dans la promotion des produits locaux ? M. Sandah : Absolument. Les produits locaux occupent une place importante dans notre alimentation et dans notre patrimoine culinaire. Les chefs peuvent les valoriser à travers des menus variés qui mettent en avant les produits de nos terroirs, les légumes et les fruits de saison ainsi que les recettes traditionnelles. Mais la promotion du consommer local doit aller de pair avec le respect des règles d’hygiène et de conservation. Un produit local doit être sélectionné, conservé et préparé dans de bonnes conditions, comme tout autre aliment. La qualité et la sécurité des mets sont essentielles pour encourager durablement la consommation locale. ATOP : Quel message aux consommateurs qui hésitent à manger dans les restaurants par crainte des risques sanitaires ? M. Sandah : Nous devons leur faire comprendre que la sécurité alimentaire est au cœur de notre métier. Les chefs cuisiniers doivent constamment améliorer leurs pratiques, renforcer leurs compétences et veiller à la qualité des produits qu’ils utilisent. La confiance du client se construit par le sérieux, l’hygiène et le respect des exigences professionnelles. Nous invitons donc les acteurs de la restauration à assumer pleinement leurs responsabilités. Les consommateurs doivent pouvoir manger au restaurant avec confiance, tout en sachant que cette confiance doit être méritée chaque jour. La promotion des produits du terroir et du savoir-faire culinaire togolais doit nécessairement s’accompagner du respect des règles d’hygiène et de sécurité alimentaire. Les chefs cuisiniers doivent veiller à la qualité des ingrédients utilisés et aux conditions de préparation des mets. Il est important de rassurer les consommateurs sur la qualité sanitaire des repas servis dans les restaurants afin de renforcer leur confiance et de les encourager à consommer davantage les produits locaux. Propos recueillis par Abel OZIH

items.title: Former GRASAG-National PRO Solomon Ametor elected NDC Deputy Secretary for Ketu North
items.description: Former Public Relations Officer of the Graduate Students’ Association of Ghana (GRASAG-National), Solomon Ametor, has been elected Deputy Secretary of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) in the Ketu North Constituency. Ametor secured 601 votes to win the position in the party’s 2026 constituency elections. He defeated three other contenders — John Dordoe, who polled 400 votes; David Kwabla Amegayie, who secured 164 votes; and Michael Doe Kporfor, who obtained 168 votes. Before he was elected NDC Deputy Secretary, Mr Ametor served as the PRO of GRASAG-National, representing and communicating the interests of graduate students at the national level. GRASAG’s official website identified him in that capacity in a May 2026 notice for the association’s national handing-over ceremony. His election forms part of the new NDC constituency executive team expected to oversee the party’s activities and mobilisation in Ketu North. Godwin Kwasi Tovor was elected Constituency Chairman after polling 818 votes against Stephen Akpabli’s 512 votes. Kodzo Bright also won the Vice Chairman position with 561 votes, while Daniel Cudjoe Esime Kporha was elected Secretary unopposed. The constituency elections were held as part of the NDC’s 2026 internal elections to select executives to lead the party at the grassroots level.
