items.title: He Wanted to Save Children. Instead, He Unleashed Chaos.
items.description: Editor's Note: This story is one in a three-part series commemorating the 10-year anniversary of Pizzagate, a conspiracy theory that led to a shooting at the Washington, D.C., restaurant Comet Ping Pong in 2016. Read Kaitlyn Tiffany’s analysis on the legacy of Pizzagate and Ross Andersen’s story about Comet Ping Pong . I n the video, recorded from the dashboard of his Toyota Prius, he looks at times like he’s on the verge of tears. Edgar Maddison Welch makes a point to look into the camera when he speaks. That’s because the video is for his two children. He speaks slowly; it’s unclear whether he’s weighing each word or simply unsure of what to say. Somewhere in the back of the car are the AR-15, the shotgun, and the .38-caliber revolver he’s brought with him. “I can’t let you grow up in a world that’s so corrupted by evil without at least standing up for you, and for other children,” he says. His demeanor is calm and there’s resignation in his voice. “Like I’ve always told you, we have a duty to protect people who can’t protect themselves and do for people who can’t do for themselves. That’s what I’m trying to do. I hope you understand that one day.” Back home in Salisbury, North Carolina, his girlfriend was not pleased. He’d left the children with her early that morning, while she was still asleep. He’d texted her that he loved her, and she’d responded with a barrage of angry replies; “idk what the fuck Ur doing it’s really starting to freak me out,” she’d written. “Jus know that the ppl u love R suffering too back home.” This impromptu six-hour road trip was nothing more than a “selfish lil adventure.” He did not see it that way. This was God’s work. Not long after leaving home, he’d texted a friend a verse from the Book of Isaiah: “He has sent me to comfort the brokenhearted and to proclaim that captives will be released and prisoners will be freed.” Tattooed on his back was a different verse from the same book—that “those who hope in the Lord” will be made strong in his image. “They will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not be faint.” Welch, who went by his middle name, Maddison, must have felt, in that moment, like he was living the scripture. Near the end of his journey, he texted his friends, asking them to take care of his family. Finally, around 3 p.m. on December 4, 2016, he arrived at his destination: a family pizza restaurant in an affluent neighborhood of Washington, D.C. He left his phone in the car but brought the guns. Holding an assault rifle across his chest, the 28-year-old walked through the front door of Comet Ping Pong in search of something that didn’t exist. The employees and families dining inside who saw him enter panicked and scrambled to leave. Just 24 minutes later, Welch walked out the same door, unarmed, with his hands in the air. Nobody had been hurt, but something had suddenly changed. Welch had gone to Comet Ping Pong to look for proof of a global elite-pedophile ring in the basement. He’d been watching YouTube videos from online shock jocks, who suggested that Comet was the site of untold horrors. It made him feel sick. Maybe he thought he would come across a hidden room full of shackled children, or a network of tunnels. Perhaps, as the conspiracies suggested, he’d catch the Clinton or Podesta families in some grotesque act. The scenario he hadn’t prepared himself for was the one in which he found nothing at all. After firing three shots at the lock of the storage-closet door, Welch saw that it contained no secret room, no ring, no conspiracy. The story of Welch, the Pizzagate shooter, as it is often told, is that of a man searching for a revelation that never arrived. But that’s not true. Welch experienced a genuine epiphany: It seems that, after entering, he could no longer deny the reality that Comet was, as any reasonable person could see, just a regular restaurant. Faced with the truth, he peacefully surrendered to police. Those following the news experienced a revelation, too, only the opposite: Welch represented an incursion of a dark, lawless online world of lies into our reality. Ten years ago, this reckless act felt more like a glitch of internet-addled, lone-wolf vigilantism. Over time, Welch has become a sadly familiar archetype—a poster boy for a long-running crisis that includes QAnon and January 6. In the aftermath of Welch’s arrest, the gunman famously told The New York Times , “The intel on this wasn’t 100 percent.” He didn’t know it then, but the phrase would turn out to be a solid epitaph for our paranoid and turbulent times. “W e are a family of rescuers,” Welch’s mother, Terri Welch, wrote in a statement shortly after the shooting. Those who knew the family described her and the shooter’s father, Harry Welch, to me as both religious and civic-minded. Terri had become a volunteer firefighter in her mid-50s, and Harry Sr. seems to have done it all. According to his IMDb page, in addition to being a screenwriter, Harry Sr. was an NRA firearms instructor who taught gun-safety classes to elementary-school students; a foster parent; and a former member of drug task forces. He claims he has held seven Guinness World Records, only one of which could I find any evidence of: a 1986 record for most consecutive one-armed push-ups. While Welch was growing up, Harry Sr. served as executive director of Protect-A-Child, a nonprofit organization for preventing child abuse and abduction. The family ran an animal rescue too. Christian Dionne, Welch’s childhood friend, told me that their house was a “wild place,” full of dozens of dogs, as well as exotic and taxidermied animals, including at least one tiger. Maddison—his friends sometimes called him Momo—had a magnetic personality. He was known to be easygoing and open. He was “the epitome of cool” even at a young age, Dionne said. A goofball obsessed with early-aughts shows such as Jackass and punch-you-in-the-nuts humor, he was privately nerdy. On weekend nights, Welch’s friends would hangout at Harry Sr.’s store for LAN parties, where they played Counter-Strike until the early hours. Welch was, according to Dionne, “very into weapons” and had scythes and throwing stars. From what can be gleaned from court records and those who knew him, Welch’s life after high school suggests an optimistic, though frenetic personality. He was prone to taking bold action like his parents: In the fall of 2009, he embarked on an impulsive, poorly timed hike of the difficult, 500-mile Colorado Trail. A local newspaper interviewed him about his adventure, depicting him as indefatigable, energized by braving blizzard conditions and even fending off a bear. In 2010, he flew down to Haiti for three weeks with a church group after a devastating earthquake and helped rebuild an orphanage. According to the pastor who accompanied him, he became so invested in the kids that he would “forgo eating and give his food to the children.” Welch surfed, hiked, and hung out with family, but he mostly seemed aimless. His employment history was spotty. “I had the impression he was basically kind of homeless for these periods,” Demian Ahn, the lead prosecutor in Welch’s case, told me. He was raising his two kids as a single parent. Some years later, he joined the local fire department as a volunteer firefighter and began working toward a paid role. And then, 41 days before his arrest at Comet, on the way to his job at a grocery warehouse, Welch hit a boy with his Buick LeSabre. Thirteen-year-old Kenyatta Belton was badly injured and airlifted to the hospital. Welch, who was driving the speed limit and not impaired, reportedly stayed with Belton at the scene. The accident, Welch’s parents told a reporter, changed his behavior. Belton survived, but it’s easy to imagine Welch drawing a parallel to a much earlier incident in his life—something he’d never talked about, according to a friend. In 1997, just before Welch turned 9, his brother, Harry Jr., died in a car accident. After the incident with Belton, according to The Washington Post , Welch suffered nightmares and was racked with guilt. He grew anxious and moody, and it seems like his life soon began to unravel. He was caring for his children during the day and working 12-hour shifts at night. At some point, the fire department removed Welch from its roster for being inactive. Illustration by Joan Wong. Source: Gage Skidmore / ZUMA Press Wire / Reuters. T he narrative that developed after the Pizzagate shooting was that Welch was something of a hyper-online lunatic. But compared with many of the extremists who followed, Welch had a scant online footprint. The 2009 local-news article about his hiking expedition mentions, with no other context, that the trip had “broken his addiction to the Internet.” Still, Welch had little more than a Facebook page. The Daily Beast reported that he’d “liked” a Facebook page for Alex Jones’s former conspiracy site, Infowars. Welch later told The New York Times that he thought Jones “touches on some issues that are viable but goes off the deep end.” Ahn, who had access to Welch’s internet history, told me that he saw a high volume of online activity in the lead-up to the shooting, especially on Facebook Messenger. “His brain was moving so fast to try and connect dots to make sense of things and with a very undisciplined religiosity,” he said. Available court records, which include data collected from Welch’s phone, show one multihour online binge on the evening of December 1, 2016—mostly YouTube, Messenger, and lots of texting. Welch told reporters that he’d first heard of Pizzagate through word of mouth. The conspiracy theory had surfaced online just before the 2016 presidential election; trolls and vigilante Reddit investigators had seized on leaked emails from Hillary Clinton’s campaign manager, John Podesta, and were suggesting that Washington elites had organized an elaborate child-trafficking ring that ran through places such as Comet Ping Pong. In court evidence, you can see that Welch had sent friends links to feverish videos about Pizzagate that have since been taken down. In one, Jones tells his audience, “You have to go investigate it for yourself.” Another Infowars video explicitly references Comet Ping Pong and ends by calling out its owner, James Alefantis: “Either you are the unlucky victim of a fake-news onslaught [due to your own poorly initiated publicity] or a decades-old pedophile ring operating in the power-hoarding shadows of Washington, D.C., is about to be opened from your front door.” Four days after sending the video, Welch walked through that front door. Three months later, he pleaded guilty to interstate transportation of firearms and ammunition, and assault with a dangerous weapon. At his trial, his friends and family spoke to his character, spirituality, and devoted parenting. Comet Ping Pong employees delivered emotional testimony about their post-traumatic stress and how Welch had shaken their community with violence. Some offered their empathy to Welch, who apologized at his sentencing but did not explicitly renounce Pizzagate. Welch was sentenced to 48 months in prison. And, on May 28, 2020, he was released into the early months of the pandemic. His life, or what can be gleaned from it through social media and news reports, seemed to follow two paths at once. The first shows a man embracing his second chance: Welch got a job at a restaurant and reunited with his girlfriend—the one he’d left with the kids. The pair had two children together after his release. Welch appears to have made a new Facebook account, using the name “Eddie Wood.” Photos on his and his girlfriend’s profiles show Welch quite active: hiking with his family, smiling with his parents at a Christmas carnival, attending a comics convention. He appears consistently happy—always making funny faces for the camera. Scrolling through the idyllic posts, I was reminded of a quote he’d given to his hometown paper in 2009: “I can’t imagine what the rest of the world offers.” Welch’s second path is documented via police blotters and obituaries. In February 2024, Welch and his girlfriend were arrested early one morning. Welch was booked after a cop found heroin and drug paraphernalia in his car; his girlfriend received extra charges for hiding meth on her during their jail booking. In his mug shot, Welch appears disheveled, his eyes nearly closed. On Christmas Day 2024, Welch was booked by Kannapolis, North Carolina, police for a failure to appear in court for possession of drug paraphernalia. And then, on January 4, 2025, police stopped a vehicle that Welch was riding in. The officer—the same one who had arrested him a few days earlier—recognized Welch and approached his door. Welch pulled out a handgun and pointed it at the officer. Officers told him to drop the weapon. He did not. The officers opened fire. Welch was taken to the hospital, where he died from gunshot wounds on January 6. W hat is somebody supposed to do with the entirety of Welch’s awful story? It’s possible to see Welch as little more than a selfish bully. Or a sad sack, a once-popular kid who peaked in high school, who didn’t get out and then watched his life fall apart. Maybe he was a dupe who immediately realized he was wrong after going too far. A devoted dad led astray by the lies of others, or a religious nut who abandoned his girlfriend and children after watching some YouTube videos. Ten years on, as I’ve pored over the contents of his ruined life and spoken with the few people who were willing to relive the story with a reporter, all that’s clear is how little Welch, the man, means to Pizzagate. When he failed to give conspiracy theorists the evidence they craved that day, they dubbed him a crisis actor. He was neither memorialized nor remembered, other than as a harbinger of the darkness that might follow in the then-new Trump era. The only thing that made him newsworthy at all was the potential violence he’d been prepared to carry out. His legacy may be best captured by a portion of the original URL of the Daily Beast ’s story about the shooting: fake-news-delivers-real-gunman . What exactly did the Pizzagate movement mean to Welch? Ahn, the prosecutor, told me he believed that Welch’s fears and anger around Pizzagate were genuine. Unlike a lot of other modern shooters, who seem to be performing for an online audience, he didn’t film his attack, and it doesn’t appear that he did it for clout. Nor does it seem like Welch made any attempts to capitalize on his infamy with the Pizzagate crowd. He seems to have been a true believer. And yet, there is no record that he continued with the cause after prison. When he got out, he went back to his life in Salisbury. For the rest of society, Welch primarily functioned as a model for the rise of a type of guy who, faced with his own unmooring, finds momentary purpose in a durable, networked fantasy. “If you don’t have a whole lot going on in your life, we’ve seen people can get so wrapped up in these narratives that they start acting as if they’re real,” Logan Strain, a co-host of the QAnon Anonymous podcast, told me. “It becomes this participatory soap opera.” Two years after Welch entered Comet Ping Pong, Matthew Wright barricaded a bridge to the Hoover Dam with an armored vehicle, holding a sign that read Release the OIG report, referring to a set of documents that QAnon believers thought would expose Democrats engaging in criminal and conspiratorial behavior. Then there was Cesar Sayoc—a man who sent 16 pipe bombs to CNN, as well as Barack Obama, Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton, and other politicians critical of Donald Trump. His van, discovered at the time of his arrest, was covered in 4chan-style memes. The Tree of Life shooter, Robert Bowers, was posting on the alt-right social network Gab up until opening fire in the synagogue. David DePape, who had been obsessed with Pizzagate and QAnon content, broke into the home of Nancy Pelosi and assaulted her husband with a hammer. These men left behind digital breadcrumbs that would become the hallmarks of a modern extremist—mounting evidence of people becoming more and more angry, frantic, and erratic until they finally take matters into their own hands. Some observers trace a straight line from Welch to the individuals who, fueled by a false belief that the 2020 election had been stolen, stormed the Capitol on January 6, 2021. “It’s all people reaching the climax of the fever dream,” Strain said. “And it starts to unravel as they cross the threshold.” When that happens, some, like Welch, lay down their weapons; others turn to unspeakable violence. The underlying dynamics behind the YouTube-to-gunman pipeline are nothing new. In his famous 1964 essay, “The Paranoid Style in American Politics,” Richard Hofstadter wrote, “We are all sufferers from history, but the paranoid is a double sufferer, since he is afflicted not only by the real world, with the rest of us, but by his fantasies as well.” The difference now is that our technology compounds and democratizes that suffering via an algorithmic feedback loop of fantasies that grow only more angry and deranged. Today, we can all be sufferers of history twice over: once by real-world violence, and again by the imagined world that the paranoid force us to attend to. Moments before Welch was sentenced, a Comet Ping Pong employee addressed the defendant directly. “I’m almost sorry you were duped,” the employee said. “That you fell into the trap of an orchestrated game created by hateful people whose intention it is to create fear and mistrust amongst the public. I’m almost sorry that the same people that inspired you to travel from North Carolina and come to my place of work with an assault rifle now believe you’re a hired actor. That’s how misinformation works and the game is played.” There’s grace in those words. They also illustrate the cycle of suffering bestowed on those who choose to submit to lies. Pizzagate didn’t end when Welch found nothing. To the conspiracy machine he briefly served, he was ultimately little more than a useful idiot, grist for the mill. His death eight years later made only brief headlines, overshadowed by the anniversary of the Capitol riots and a forthcoming Trump inauguration. Many of those who had trafficked the lies that led Welch to Comet Ping Pong didn’t even note his passing. Welch’s is a particularly American tragedy. “Maddison was always, especially after his brother died, looking for something to believe in,” Dionne, his childhood friend, told me. And so Edgar Maddison Welch entered a pizza parlor hoping to find a monster. Turns out, it was him.

items.title: The Epstein-Pizzagate Connection
items.description: Editor's Note: This story is one in a three-part series commemorating the 10-year anniversary of Pizzagate, a conspiracy theory that led to a shooting at the Washington, D.C., restaurant Comet Ping Pong in 2016. Read Ross Andersen’s story about Comet Ping Pong and Charlie Warzel’s profile of the Pizzagate shooter , Edgar Maddison Welch. E arlier this year, on his very popular podcast, Tucker Carlson brought up a “semi-forgotten story” that he had once found absurd. “I didn’t take Pizzagate as seriously, maybe, as I guess I should have at the time,” he said. The time he was referring to is the late fall of 2016, just before and after the first election of Donald Trump, when the details of an imagined pedophilia ring that was organized by powerful Democrats began to spread online. The Pizzagate conspiracy theory was drawn from a batch of hacked emails from Hillary Clinton’s campaign chairman, John Podesta, who had corresponded with the owner of a Washington, D.C., pizza restaurant called Comet Ping Pong. Podesta had sent a bunch of emails about pizza. It’s not worth your time for me to explain why some people became convinced that these were full of coded references to child sex slaves. The important thing to know or remember is that, by early December, the theory was spilling over into practice. Edgar Welch, a 28-year-old North Carolina man, arrived at Comet one Sunday afternoon with a revolver and an AR-15, under the assumption that he would find and free the children being kept there. Now everyone could see that the aspersion-casting had gone too far. One of the leading Pizzagate influencers, Alex Jones, publicly apologized to Comet’s owner, presumably to avoid a lawsuit , and one of Trump’s favored far-right influencers, Jack Posobiec—a guy who had once barged into the restaurant himself, with a camera rolling—backed off too, eventually insisting that he had never even claimed the conspiracy was real. Pizzagate had become embarrassing, even to its early promoters. But any trace of shame is now a distant memory. Ten years after its inception, Carlson is interested in Pizzagate—and regretful that he wasn’t interested before. In this, he’s not alone. Last January, when the government released millions of pages of files related to the crimes of Jeffrey Epstein, one subset of internet sleuths began by searching them for mentions of “pizza.” They found many. On his podcast, Carlson said he was intrigued by several in which Epstein and his urologist discussed going out for “pizza and grape soda,” a combination that Carlson found so absurd as to be suspicious. “Maybe this is code,” he said. Carlson’s guest, an up-and-coming conspiracy-theory YouTuber named Ian Carroll, encouraged him to keep thinking. What if Welch’s storming of the pizzeria was not, after all, a sad example of the internet’s power to mislead, but rather something else: a cover-up? Sure, Welch had burst into Comet and terrorized the customers and employees within, but not a single person had been physically harmed (convenient). Welch’s bullets did end up damaging a computer (convenient), which may have contained who knows what kind of information (convenient). After Welch was arrested, he gave (convenient) quotes to reporters about how he’d been misled by online sources. That neat story, Carroll implied, had been designed to make it seem like any question-asking along the lines of Pizzagate was dangerous and wrong. Carlson seemed convinced. When the interview went up on YouTube (where it currently has 2.7 million views), the video description read, “It looks like Pizzagate is basically real.” The same conclusion has in recent years been percolating throughout mainstream social-media platforms, where moderation rules once restricted discussion of Pizzagate. Following the Welch incident, nearly all of them made some effort to block Pizzagate-related hashtags or at least add warning labels to Pizzagate-related content—but these measures are no longer in place. “It’s become en vogue to revisit this theory,” Samuel Woolley, an associate professor and chair in disinformation studies at the University of Pittsburgh, told me. Back in 2016, Pizzagate was interpreted as a close call and taken as a warning. It was a sign that any of the turbid fantasies that swirl around in online spaces might lap across the boundary with real life. But the shocking power of that revelation—drawn from an episode in which nobody got hurt and the shooter apologized—is hard to fathom now. More thorough bendings of reality have long since become the norm, and the barrier between the online and offline worlds is all but gone. W hen government prosecutors asked that Edgar Welch be given 54 months in prison for his pizza-joint invasion, they cited the need to “deter other would-be vigilantes from attempting similar crimes against innocent subjects of the next internet-inspired conspiracy theory.” They said they thought it was important to make sure that such a weird thing never happened again. Demian Ahn, who served as one of those prosecutors, told me that the sum total of all of the evidence in the case—what was on Welch’s phone, what his friends and family had said in interviews—indicated that Welch’s motivations were sincere. He really thought that he was going to be saving children from the basement of a pizza place. “He seemed to be a well-meaning person,” Ahn said. “He believed that Washington, D.C., as a city, was so corrupt that you could have a child-exploitation ring openly operated by prominent people at a regular restaurant.” How exactly Welch had come to this belief would be the subject of various postmortems in the years that followed. These did not agree on where and how the Pizzagate story gained its crucial momentum: Some experts said that anonymous posters on 4chan drove the theory’s spread; others claimed that ordinary Facebook users played the most important role. Russian propagandists certainly were involved, eagerly reposting #Pizzagate content, but so were right-wing influencers in the United States. However it emerged, Pizzagate did fade for a while after Welch’s arrest, before returning in expanded form with QAnon . That sprawling belief system took hold near the end of Trump’s first term, and imagined the president as an avenging angel, bringing violent justice to a network of Satanic Democrats who were after children’s blood. When social platforms cracked down on QAnon in 2020 and 2021, on account of its connection to the storming of the Capitol, the Pizzagate theory got tamped down once again. But it never really went away. Trump campaigned for his second term in part by incorporating QAnon slogans and themes into his messaging. Today’s Pizzagate believers take a broader view than Welch did. As Samuel Woolley put it, they may not claim that all of the details of the theory were right on target—that there really was a basement full of trafficked children in a pizza place in D.C.—“but that the general thrust of the argument was correct.” (When Carlson and Carroll riffed on the theory, this is how they talked.) Many people now assert that Epstein started Pizzagate himself, to draw attention away from his own child-sex-related crimes, Woolley told me. They point suggestively to evidence that Epstein once met with 4chan’s founder . Carlson, too, seems preoccupied with Epstein’s connection to Pizzagate. I reached out to him this fall, and when we spoke by phone, he kept returning to the same text-message exchange that he’d cited on his podcast, between Epstein and the billionaire’s urologist. “No rich white person drinks grape soda, period,” Carlson said. “Grape soda is probably more unfashionable than cigarettes among rich people. I just want to say that unequivocally. Where do you even buy grape soda?” Any reference to it in the texts was obviously code for something , he insisted. He just didn’t know for what. T oday’s conspiracy theories are ornate. They animate online communities of all different political bents and cultural referents, and they overlap in surprising and strange ways. Take Ian Carroll, the guest on Carlson’s podcast, who is better known for filling in as the host of Candace Owens’s show while she was on maternity leave. He has launched an interactive tool called the “Webb,” which allows evidence from disparate public sources to be pieced together. Anyone can use his string-board engine to connect documents from the Epstein files to those concerning, among other things, UFOs, 9/11, the Zodiac Killer, and the murder of Charlie Kirk. (Carroll did not respond to requests for an interview.) A site like that may still be somewhat of a niche concern, but a paranoid attitude has clearly become more widespread in our culture since 2016. An attempted assassination at the White House Correspondent’s Dinner, a flood in Texas , or a football team’s failure —none are necessarily accepted as what they seem. The facts themselves may not always matter so much as the thrill of riffing and guessing. At one point in the Pizzagate episode of his podcast, Carlson told Carroll that he thought he’d heard that the shooter ended up getting killed right before the Epstein files came out. “Is that true?” he asked. “I heard the same reporting,” Carroll said. “Obviously, at this point, I don’t really know what’s true. The whole world feels a little bit like The Matrix .” In fact, the timeline is unambiguous: Edgar Welch was shot and killed by police in January 2025 after pointing a gun at an officer during a traffic stop; the Epstein files were released in December of that year. Later, when I spoke with Carlson on the phone, he explained that he’d disregarded Pizzagate originally because he’d been too close to it. Literally, he’d lived near Comet and taken his children there for pizza. He knew John Podesta, his brother, and his brother’s wife personally, and he knew the pizza-shop owner too. “It seemed so far-out, I don’t think I spent 10 minutes thinking about it.” Now he lives in Maine and eats gas-station pizza, he told me. And he is very confused as to why the Epstein files’ references to pizza and grape soda haven’t gotten more attention from media and law enforcement. “Everyone is effectively covering for Epstein—why?” he said. “I don’t know the answer.” After we hung up, I reasoned that it was fair to ask a journalist to look into this matter, so I did. Epstein and his urologist talked about pizza and grape soda at least five times in 2018, the year before Epstein’s death. I couldn’t reach the urologist by phone to ask why. But on one occasion , he’d accompanied his text with a photo. He was in a pizza shop, having a cheese slice with a bottle of Crush grape soda. *Illustration source: Mugshot Zone

items.title: The Long, Weird Tale of Comet Ping Pong
items.description: Editor's Note: This story is one in a three-part series commemorating the 10-year anniversary of Pizzagate, a conspiracy theory that led to a shooting at the Washington, D.C., restaurant Comet Ping Pong in 2016. Read Kaitlyn Tiffany’s analysis on the legacy of Pizzagate and Charlie Warzel’s profile of the Pizzagate shooter , Edgar Maddison Welch. J ames Alefantis had an excruciating hangover when he first learned that his restaurant, Comet Ping Pong, was the suspected site of a global sex-trafficking organization. It was late October 2016, and he’d just thrown a 10-year anniversary party for the Washington, D.C., pizzeria. There had been much to celebrate: After grinding through a few slow years, Comet had become a favorite among families in the city’s prosperous Northwest quadrant and also, improbably, an important venue for punk bands. Alefantis had hired a band to play the party and, like many of the hundreds of guests who showed up, he overindulged at the open bar. The next morning, he was barely conscious when his general manager called to say that a reporter had been in touch with some questions about a thing called “Pizzagate.” Alefantis was, as you might imagine, surprised to hear that people on 4chan and Reddit had identified Comet’s basement—which does not exist—as the headquarters of a pedophilia ring run by Bill and Hillary Clinton. “It sounded like the dumbest thing ever,” he told me earlier this month. The theory was based on a bizarre reading of leaked emails sent by John Podesta, who was the chair of Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign at the time, and knew Alefantis socially. Cheese pizza was said to be Podesta’s code word for “child pornography,” and pasta his word for “little boy.” Wikileaks Excerpt from a leaked email to John Podesta from December 2015 with the header “Cheese.” Alefantis’s first instinct was to brush it off. He figured that Pizzagate was just another one of those downs that tend to follow ups in the restaurant business, like when you have a great weekend and then on Monday, your hood fan goes on the fritz. People say lots of crazy things online, especially when the national mood is inflamed by a presidential election. After Donald Trump won a few days later, Alefantis allowed himself to hope that the fever would break. Jason Andrew for The Atlantic Comet Ping Pong’s owner, James Alefantis, sits for a portrait in a booth at the restaurant on October 23, 2026. T he decor at Comet can be bewildering for first-time visitors. The dining room is dominated by an enormous, fire-breathing pizza oven. A mint-green Vespa hangs, inexplicably, from the ceiling, alongside glowing neon tubes and globe lights. The densely packed two-tops and four-tops beneath it are painted green and white to look like miniature Ping-Pong tables. Alefantis has two actual Ping-Pong tables in the back; he put them in when, after leasing the space, he realized that he could afford to renovate only its front half. In a room behind the Ping-Pong area, I sat down with Erika Mendoza, Comet’s general manager. Through the wall, we could hear a ball bouncing back and forth between a father’s and son’s paddles, and their occasional yelps of frustration or triumph. Mendoza, who is 35, has worked at Comet since she was 19. She was working as a host when the Pizzagate theory first surfaced, and she remembers the staff joking about it. But then, over the course of November, their mood darkened. Trump’s victory didn’t placate the conspiracy’s true believers, as Alefantis had hoped. Instead, it seemed to embolden them. The restaurant’s phone line was deluged with fake orders, screamed obscenities, and threatened violence. A few people came in and started nosing around. The far-right influencer Jack Posobiec was thrown out after he tried to record a child’s birthday party. For some, being visibly connected to Comet meant becoming a target on social media. The married lesbian couple who supplies the restaurant’s pickles were accused of kidnapping their own child. Regular customers who interacted with Comet’s social accounts suddenly found hateful comments directed toward them. Mendoza remembers a staffer openly wondering whether someone might soon come in with a gun. Jason Andrew for The Atlantic Artwork adorns the walls inside the dining room. On Sunday, December 4, Mendoza was getting ready for her evening shift when her phone rang. One of Comet’s servers was on the line, who told Mendoza not to come in. Pizzagate had roused powerful feelings in a troubled man named Edgar Welch, and earlier that day, he had driven all the way to Comet from North Carolina on a mission to find and liberate the restaurant’s purported child sex slaves. Welch had parked nearby and walked in with a loaded Colt revolver in a holster and a black assault rifle strapped across his chest. As he made a beeline toward the back, a Comet staffer caught a glimpse of the AR-15 and proceeded to shoo his colleagues and customers out the front door. The police arrived and barricaded off an entire block of Connecticut Avenue. Welch roamed the restaurant until he found a locked door. It led to a closet containing Comet’s soda system, point-of-sale computer, and some light bulbs, but he didn’t know that. He fired his AR-15 into the door, splintering the wood. By the time Alefantis, who had been grabbing coffee across town, arrived at the neighborhood firehouse where his employees had been evacuated, Welch had already surrendered. “The intel on this wasn’t 100 percent,” the gunman later said. That evening, when the police took crime-scene photos in Comet, the restaurant looked downright eerie. On the tables and at the bar, pizzas sat half-eaten next to translucent red cups full of water, the ice in them having melted hours before. After night fell, a detective let Alefantis inside. He was unsettled by the stillness. He remembers thinking that Comet would probably have to close its doors for good. Miraculously, no one had gotten hurt, but this conspiracy theory had unleashed real-world forces that were powerful enough to stamp out his little restaurant. Who would want to come eat at a place where another gunman might soon show up? A lot of people, it turned out. That night, the phone was already starting to ring, and when Alefantis picked up, he found customers on the line. They wanted to know when the restaurant would reopen. The next day, Alefantis held a meeting with the staff. Friends had urged him to make a trauma therapist available, and he took their advice. He asked everyone whether they wanted to keep Comet operational. One by one, servers, bartenders, and runners said yes. Mendoza told me that she offered to host. She remembers the phones ringing off the hook during the meeting. Still more people were calling to ask when they could come in. “I was like, ‘I guess we’ll fucking open!’” Alefantis told me. His voice still cracks when he talks about the next day. Overnight, customers had dropped off signs, flowers, and cards, including some containing cash that was earmarked for staff drinks. For the first dinner shift, they massed outside, forming a line that stretched down the block. Human group behavior exists on a spectrum, and for a month, Comet’s staff had experienced the hateful end of it. During the reopening, they experienced the other end. “I saw all of these regulars,” Mendoza told me. “They waited hours just to get a table, and then they waited another hour to get their pizza because we were so overwhelmed.” Jason Andrew for The Atlantic Comet Ping Pong’s general manager, Erika Mendoza, 35, stands for a portrait in the back of the restaurant. H ow nice it would be to end this story right there, to report that this bizarre upwelling of conspiracy and violence culminated in a happily-ever-after for all involved. But that’s not what happened. After Welch was arrested, few of Pizzagate’s true believers issued mea culpas and abandoned their darker imaginings about the restaurant. Instead, they incorporated his arrest into the conspiracy theory, as true believers are wont to do. On online forums, they would later suggest that the whole episode was a staged hoax, a false flag intended to throw them off the scent. Within days of Comet’s reopening, the hostile phone calls started up again. The staff were so often told that they would burn in the fires of hell that they stopped answering out-of-state numbers. Then they started receiving robocalls from local lines. When Mendoza was away from work, even in her sleep, she would hear phantom ringing. Alefantis decided to disconnect the phones altogether. Many staffers had to lock down their social-media accounts too. Alefantis changed his cell-phone number. In his email inbox, he continually received security alerts, triggered by attempted hacks of Comet’s website. One anonymous emailer sent Alefantis shaky video footage of the exterior of his house. The restaurant entered its fortress era. Alefantis hired a pair of armed guards for the front door and locked the back entrance, which had previously been open to a parking lot. He had panic buttons installed inside the restaurant, and security cameras placed in each of its rooms. He called D.C.’s chief of police and arranged for squad cars to be parked at two locations near the restaurant, to deter any Welch copycats. In a sop to conspiracy theorists who might show up, the staff started keeping the door to the back room open, and they made sure the lights were always switched on. That way, anyone could see that no child torture was taking place. Ahead of Welch’s sentencing, in June 2017, several staffers gave victim statements to the court. One reported having frequent flashbacks, and said that they couldn’t help obsessing over how differently things might have gone that day if they hadn’t been able to escape the restaurant. Another said that their family and friends had only recently resumed speaking to them like a normal person, “and not some spectacle to gawk at.” According to Mendoza, several employees quit. There was no lasting fix for problems of this sort. Comet’s staff could only treat them one by one, with short-term interventions. During the Women’s March in 2017, members of the Westboro Baptist Church launched a protest outside the restaurant. They held up signs with homophobic messages, including one that said GOT AIDS YET? They used a megaphone to call Alefantis an anti-gay slur. This gave him an idea. Being a small concert venue, Comet has some pretty serious loudspeakers. The staff wheeled them out and played Lady Gaga loud enough to drown out the protesters. (Alefantis also brought them flutes of champagne, but this peace offering was refused.) The tactic worked so well that Comet would use it again when the Official Street Preachers, another hate group, later picketed the restaurant. It was a big hit with customers. Jason Andrew for The Atlantic Guests watch a performance by Saoires Dream at the restaurant. In January 2019, violence struck Comet again. A young man named Ryan Jaselskis came in and ordered three beers at the bar. (An hour before arriving, he’d uploaded a video to YouTube in which he proclaimed that the world is run by a satanic global pedophile ring.) After finishing his last beer, he left a generous tip, alongside a diaper and some baby food. Then he walked to the back of the restaurant, poured lighter fluid on its curtains, and set them on fire. Two staffers doused the flames with help from a customer. Like other restaurants, Comet faced tough times during the pandemic, but the intense public focus on the coronavirus at least seemed to draw away some of the negative attention. For months, only staff were allowed inside; as a consequence, security became less of a concern. Employees busied themselves with to-go orders, making Comet’s signature pizzas, such as the hottie (pepperoni and jalapeños) and the smoky (smoked mozzarella, smoked bacon, and smoked mushrooms). When Comet finally reopened for dine-in, the atmosphere wasn’t as charged. Many of its former tormentors seemed to have moved on. But even now, the staff is vigilant. They still get calls here and there, Mendoza told me. People will ask, “Where’s the basement?” or something similar. In place of full-time security, the restaurant has developed certain protocols. New employees are told to stay cognizant of their surroundings. They try to discourage Pizzagate tourism. Anyone who walks in and starts recording video is quickly approached, and many are asked to leave. Comet’s booking agent asks the bands and stand-up comics who perform to refrain from riffing on Pizzagate from the stage. Sometimes people still show up looking for trouble. Last year, a few men rolled in, and Mendoza felt that something was off about them. (A decade of such incidents has trained her senses.) Sure enough, one in the group was wearing a shirt that said Pizzagate is real . After they started saying offensive stuff to a waiter, Mendoza threw them out and called the police. Then she called Alefantis. He picked up right away. He told me that he’s never without his phone. Alefantis emphasized that Comet’s story isn’t a sad one. These days, mean-spirited visitors don’t show up as often. Staffers are no longer constantly besieged by callers who wish them ill. Nor is the restaurant a haunted or tragic place. The people who work there seem to care about one another. Several employees and former employees have had their wedding ceremonies and receptions at the restaurant. For them, the place is so much bigger than this crazy invented story about it. And the Pizzagate anniversary isn’t the only one on their calendar. As of this month, Comet has been in business for 20 years. Alefantis told me that planning for the party is already under way.

items.title: SIAO 2026: SITARAIL offre un train gratuit aux artisans du Guiriko
items.description: À Bobo-Dioulasso, SITARAIL a lancé, le mercredi 28 octobre 2026, le «train de l’artisanat», une navette ferroviaire gratuite destinée aux artisans de la région du Guiriko et à leurs marchandises pour leur permettre de rallier Ouagadougou, à l’occasion du Salon international de l’artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO). Plus de 300 places sont disponibles pour cette opération, qui prévoit l’acheminement d’environ 282 tonnes de marchandises vers la capitale burkinabè. Participer au SIAO représente souvent un défi logistique et financier pour les artisans de Bobo-Dioulasso. Entre le coût du déplacement, le transport des produits et les contraintes liées à l’acheminement des marchandises, les dépenses peuvent rapidement devenir importantes. Pour alléger ces charges et faciliter leur participation à ce rendez-vous international, SITARAIL a mis en place un dispositif exceptionnel: le «train de l’artisanat». Le secrétaire général de la région, Souleymane Nakanabo (Ph. LeFaso.net) Le lancement de cette initiative s’est déroulé à Bobo-Dioulasso, sous la présidence du secrétaire général de la région du Guiriko, Souleymane Nakanabo, représentant le gouverneur. À travers cette opération, l’entreprise ferroviaire entend offrir aux artisans une solution de transport adaptée, en leur permettant de voyager gratuitement avec leurs produits à destination de Ouagadougou. Pour cette édition, SITARAIL a mobilisé une rame entière, avec plus de 300 places disponibles. Plus d’une centaine d’artisans ont embarqué, tandis que près de 282 tonnes de marchandises doivent être acheminées vers la capitale, selon les chiffres communiqués par Alexis Ouédraogo, représentant de l’entreprise. Le représentant de SITARAIL, Alexis Ouédraogo (Ph. Lefaso.net) «Au départ, nous mettions seulement un collecteur à la disposition des artisans pour acheminer leurs articles à Ouagadougou. Cette fois-ci, nous avons décidé de passer à un autre cap en mettant toute une rame à leur disposition», a-t-il expliqué, soulignant l’évolution du soutien apporté aux acteurs de l’artisanat. Un soulagement pour les exposants Pour les bénéficiaires, cette initiative constitue une réponse concrète à l’une des principales difficultés rencontrées lors de leur participation au salon: le coût du transport des personnes et des marchandises. Ali Prospère Traoré, promoteur de l’entreprise Pro Couture, s’est réjoui de cette prise en charge, qui permet aux exposants de réduire considérablement leurs dépenses. Ali Prospère Traoré exprime sa satisfaction face à l'initiative de la SITARAIL (Ph. LeFaso.net) «Le transport est un problème pour les artisans. Pour aller au SIAO avec deux compagnons, il faut payer le déplacement de trois personnes. Le transport des bagages coûte également cher et les marchandises ne peuvent pas toujours partir en une seule fois», a déclaré M. Traoré, avant d’exprimer sa reconnaissance à SITARAIL pour cet accompagnement. Même satisfaction chez Mariam Sawadogo, couturière, promotrice d’un centre de couture et exposante au Village artisanal. Pour elle, la gratuité du transport constitue un véritable avantage, tant sur le plan financier que sur celui de l’organisation. Le train de l'artisan est un ouf de soulagement selon la couturière Mariam Sawadogo (Ph. LeFaso.net) «Nos bagages sont partis gratuitement et nous-mêmes, nous voyageons gratuitement. C’est un honneur pour nous de bénéficier de cet accompagnement. Auparavant, nous pouvions voyager sans être certains que toutes nos marchandises arriveraient à destination au moment voulu. Cette fois-ci, nos bagages sont partis avant nous. Nous sommes rassurés», a-t-elle confié. Grâce à ce dispositif, les artisans peuvent, donc, mieux organiser leur participation au SIAO, limiter les contraintes liées au transport et se concentrer davantage sur la présentation et la commercialisation de leurs produits. Les autorités régionales saluent l'initiative Présent à la cérémonie de lancement au nom du gouverneur du Guiriko, le secrétaire général de la région, Souleymane Nakanabo, a salué cette action en faveur du développement de l’artisanat et de la valorisation du patrimoine culturel burkinabè. Rendant hommage au talent et à la créativité des artisans, il a mis en avant leur contribution au rayonnement de Bobo-Dioulasso et de sa région. Des artisans prêts à embarquer à bord du train de l’artisanat (Ph. Lefaso.net) «C’est grâce à vos doigts, à vos têtes qui pensent et à votre talent que cette réalité est possible», a affirmé M. Nakanabo. Il a, par ailleurs, invité les exposants à donner le meilleur d’eux-mêmes afin de faire honneur au Guiriko durant cette manifestation internationale. Le représentant du gouverneur a également formulé le vœu que les artisans réalisent de bonnes affaires à Ouagadougou. «Notre souhait est que le train de l’artisanat, en allant, soit lourd, mais qu’au retour, il soit léger. Tout ce que vous allez amener sera payé et vous reviendrez avec l’argent», a-t-il lancé, dans un message d’encouragement aux bénéficiaires. Au-delà de l’appui logistique, la participation au SIAO représente pour les artisans une occasion de faire découvrir leurs créations, de nouer des contacts commerciaux et de conquérir de nouveaux débouchés. SITARAIL renforce son engagement culturel Le «train de l’artisanat» s’inscrit dans la continuité des initiatives mises en œuvre par SITARAIL pour accompagner les manifestations culturelles et touristiques au Burkina Faso. Après le «train de la culture», organisé dans le cadre de la Semaine nationale de la culture (SNC), et le «train du tourisme», lancé à l’occasion de la Grande saison du tourisme, l’entreprise poursuit son soutien aux acteurs de l’économie culturelle. Photo de famille (Ph. LeFaso.net) Pour Alexis Ouédraogo de SITARAIL, cette démarche traduit la volonté de sa société, membre du groupe Africa Global Logistics (AGL), de rester aux côtés des autorités et des acteurs qui contribuent au développement du pays. Il a, par ailleurs, salué la forte présence des femmes parmi les bénéficiaires et les a encouragées à profiter de la campagne Octobre rose pour se faire dépister contre le cancer du sein. En facilitant le transport des artisans et de leurs marchandises, SITARAIL entend ainsi contribuer à une participation plus accessible au SIAO 2026. Pour les exposants du Guiriko, l’enjeu est désormais de tirer pleinement profit de cette opportunité, de valoriser leur savoir-faire et de transformer leur présence à Ouagadougou en succès commerciaux. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article SIAO 2026: SITARAIL offre un train gratuit aux artisans du Guiriko est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Pakistan, China sign agreement to operationalise green channel at Sost-Khunjerab border
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and China have signed an agreement to operationalise a green channel at the Sost-Khunjerab border for agricultural and allied products to facilitate bilateral trade. The agreement was signed online between the customs administrations of the two countries at the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) on Thursday. The Pakistani delegation was led by Member Customs (Operations) Syed Shakeel Shah, while the Chinese delegation was headed by Li Qinghua, deputy head of Urumqi Customs and director of Tashkurgan Customs. According to an official announcement, the agreement aims to establish a green channel for an agreed list of agricultural products, allowing eligible consignments to undergo priority processing and examination while maintaining risk-based customs controls. The arrangement also provides for enhanced information sharing and the exchange of risk alerts between the two customs administrations to strengthen coordination and improve cross-border trade management. The agreement also provides for enhanced exchange of information and risk alerts between the two customs administrations to strengthen coordination and improve the management of cross-border trade. It further envisages priority handling of perishable consignments to minimise delays and ensure their timely movement across the border. The Pakistani delegation also included the chief collector of customs, Peshawar; the collector of customs, Gilgit-Baltistan; representatives of the Department of Plant Protection, NAFSA, Pakistan Single Window and the Ministry of Commerce; and the commercial counsellor at the Pakistan embassy in China. The operationalisation of the green channel is expected to improve the efficiency of agricultural trade and strengthen customs cooperation between the two countries. Khunjerab Pass connects Gilgit-Baltistan with China’s Xinjiang region and is the highest paved international border at 15,500 feet above sea level. Under the border protocol agreement signed between the two countries in 1985, the pass remains open for travel and trade between April and November. In winter, trade and travel are hampered by excessive snowfall. Last year, Pakistan Customs collected Rs15 billion in revenue on imports from China through the Khunjerab Pass, breaking the previous record. Goods worth Rs2.8bn were also exported to China and Central Asian countries through the border crossing.

items.title: Régularisation des sans-papiers : Me Megherbi alerte sur une « bombe à retardement dans les préfectures »
items.description: Le compte à rebours est lancé pour les travailleurs sans-papiers en France . La loi immigration du 26 janvier 2024, qui avait introduit une nouvelle voie de régularisation des travailleurs étrangers sans titre de séjour, prendra fin, sans renouvellement législatif, pour le moment, le 31 décembre 2026. Pour rappel, cette loi permet aux travailleurs étrangers exerçant dans les secteurs dits « en tension » de prétendre à un titre de séjour sous certaines conditions, sans avoir notamment à faire intervenir leur patron ni à dépendre de celui-ci pour la signature de documents administratifs. Cette mesure figure à l’article 27 de la loi, qui a créé l’article L. 435-4 du Code de l’entrée et du séjour des étrangers et du droit d’asile (CESEDA). L’arrêté du 21 mai 2025 a fixé la liste des métiers et zones géographiques caractérisés par des difficultés de recrutement. Il s’agit notamment des métiers du BTP, de l’hôtellerie, de la restauration ou encore du service à la personne. Les conditions de dépôt d’un dossier de titre de séjour sur ce fondement sont globalement les suivantes : résider en France de manière ininterrompue depuis au moins trois ans, avoir travaillé au moins douze mois et occuper un emploi dans un secteur en tension lors du dépôt du dossier en préfecture. Enfin, il faut pouvoir justifier de son insertion en France. Tous ces éléments sont examinés par la préfecture. Ce n’est donc pas, rappelons-le, un droit acquis du fait de travailler dans un secteur en tension, mais une autre voie possible de régularisation. Quelles conséquences pour ces milliers de travailleurs sans-papiers ? « Dans quelques mois, la fenêtre administrative qui leur offrait une chance d’obtenir des papiers sera définitivement close », alerte Maître Megherbi, avocat au barreau de Paris, avant d’ajouter que la fin de la mesure constitue une « bombe à retardement dans des préfectures déjà saturées ». L’engorgement des préfectures, avec des délais rallongés déjà observables, risque de s’accentuer. En effet, « alors que les délais d’obtention d’un rendez-vous en préfecture se comptent déjà en mois, attendre la fin de l’année équivaut pour beaucoup à un arrêt de mort administratif (…) C’est une véritable course contre la montre qui s’est engagée », nous explique Maître Megherbi. Son conseil : « N’attendez pas la dernière minute . Chaque semaine compte pour réunir les preuves de présence, constituer un dossier en béton et arracher un créneau de dépôt ». Les conséquences de la fin de la mesure Alors que ces secteurs peinent déjà à recruter, rendre plus difficile la régularisation de milliers d’hommes et de femmes qui contribuent à l’économie française reviendrait à les replonger dans l’illégalité. Du côté des employeurs, cela contribuerait également à prolonger les difficultés de recrutement. L’absence de renouvellement législatif constitue donc une voie de régularisation en moins pour une partie des travailleurs, et signifie, pour d’autres, un maintien dans l’illégalité. C’est pour toutes ces raisons que Me Megherbi rappelle qu’actuellement, « associations de défense des étrangers, syndicats et avocats spécialisés tirent la sonnette d’alarme et appellent à une mobilisation d’urgence ». L’article Régularisation des sans-papiers : Me Megherbi alerte sur une « bombe à retardement dans les préfectures » est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Christine Lagarde dejará la presidencia del BCE el 7 de febrero y abre la carrera por su sucesión
items.description: La silla económica más importante de Europa está vacante. La presidenta del Banco Central Europeo, Christine Lagarde, dejará su cargo el 7 de febrero, casi nueve meses antes de que venza su mandato el 31 de octubre de 2027. El movimiento, anunciado por el banco este jueves, ya estaba en los corrillos políticos y financieros de Europa desde hace meses (así lo publicaron Reuters, Bloomberg y Financial Times ) y obliga a los miembros de la eurozona a pactar en pocas semanas la renovación casi al completo de la cúpula de la institución económica más poderosa del continente. El 3 de enero abandona su puesto la alemana Isabel Schnabel , consejera del banco dedicada a mercados financieros, y el 1 de junio Philip Lane, irlandés que ejerce como economista jefe. Son los tres puestos más codiciados del comité ejecutivo del banco, órgano de gobierno de la entidad, y la decisión de Lagarde llevará a los países de la zona euro a negociar una renovación en bloque. Además, permite que sea el Gobierno francés de Emmanuel Macron quien participe en las conversaciones, antes de las elecciones presidenciales de la próxima primavera. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Court sacks Uzodinma as APC senatorial candidate for Imo West
items.description: …orders INEC to recognise ex-Gov Okorocha By Ikechukwu Nnochiri, Abuja The Federal High Court in Abuja on Thursday nullified the emergence of Governor Hope Uzodinma as candidate of the All Progressives Congress (APC) for the Imo West Senatorial election slated for January 16, 2027. The court, in a judgment delivered by Justice Obiora Egwuatu, held that evidence before it established that Governor Uzodinma was not the valid winner of the primary election the APC conducted in the senatorial zone on May 18, which was monitored by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). According to the court, it was a former governor of the state, Senator Rochas Okorocha, who garnered the highest number of votes cast at the primary election and therefore ought to have been nominated by the party. Consequently, Justice Egwuatu ordered INEC to forthwith recognise Senator Okorocha and publish his name as the authentic candidate of the APC for the senatorial poll. It further issued an order barring Governor Uzodinma from presenting himself as the candidate of the APC for the election. The post Court sacks Uzodinma as APC senatorial candidate for Imo West appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Iran Guards says three tankers on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz
items.description: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Thursday that three oil tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz. “Over the past 24 hours, three violating oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking mines while attempting to pass through the unauthorised southern route of the Strait of Hormuz,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement. The vessels had “switched off all their radar and navigation systems” and disregarded warnings from the IRGC navy, the statement said. It was not immediately clear when the incidents occurred or which flags the tankers were flying. Since the outbreak of the war on February 28, Iran has severely restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil and gas consumption. The United States has in response imposed a blockade on Iranian ports. Iran’s armed forces have repeatedly accused US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees US military operations in the region, of encouraging vessels to use a southern corridor near the Omani coast that Tehran considers unauthorised. “The IRGC Navy states that the unauthorised route through the Strait of Hormuz is mined, and that vessel owners and crews are responsible for transiting these routes and should not pay attention to CENTCOM’s delusions on social media,” the statement said. Earlier on Thursday, the British maritime agency UKMTO said it had received a report of a ship on fire in the strait but gave no details about the cause or any casualties. It was not immediately clear if it was one of the three ships referred to by the Guards. The organisation also said it had captured a US reconnaissance drone during an operation in the Strait of Hormuz in a separate statement. “The IRGC Navy announced that its electronic warfare unit had successfully captured a US MQM-170 drone during an offensive operation in the western Strait of Hormuz,” the statement said. The post Iran Guards says three tankers on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Circulation : au cœur de l’enfer routier entre Colobane et les HLM
items.description: L’axe Colobane – HLM s'est transformé en un véritable parcours du combattant. Entre nids-de-poule et mares de boue, la circulation y est devenue un calvaire. Chauffeurs, motocyclistes et commerçants crient leur exaspération face à cette route complètement dégradée. Il est un peu plus de 11 h entre le rond-point de Colobane et les HLM, et sous une chaleur écrasante, la circulation dakaroise ne s'arrête jamais. Pourtant, traverser cette rue relève aujourd'hui d'un vrai parcours du combattant : au milieu de la route, le bitume défoncé a laissé place à une grande mare d'eau boueuse qui tente de masquer vainement de profonds nids-de-poule. Aux abords des routes, les riverains ont empilé des sacs de sable pour limiter les infiltrations et offrir un passage de fortune aux piétons. Dans ce désordre, chaque déplacement demande une grande prudence : les motocyclistes louvoient sur les bandes de terre sèche, à l'image d'un conducteur en t-shirt rouge et mules jaunes qui avance au pas, le guidon chargé de paquets. Malgré le mauvais état de la voie, le trafic reste intense et montre tout le décor typique de la capitale : les symboliques « Cars Rapides » jaunes et bleus fendent les flaques avec assurance, tandis que les taxis ralentissent au maximum pour ne pas abîmer leur bas de caisse ou caler, suivis de près par des voitures prises dans d'immenses embouteillages. Sur les trottoirs encombrés, le commerce ne s'arrête pas pour autant et les vendeurs veillent simplement à protéger leurs marchandises des éclaboussures. Habitué de ce calvaire routier, Modou Dia, chauffeur de « car rapide », s’entretient avec quelques collègues et apprentis. Il saisit l’occasion pour exprimer toute sa frustration : « Nous rencontrons de graves problèmes à cause de l’état de la chaussée. Tous nos véhicules tombent en panne. C’est toujours ainsi sur cet axe reliant le rond-point de Colobane aux HLM, et cela va même bien au-delà : de la mosquée Massalikul Jinann jusqu’à Castor, la route est complètement dégradée. » Un sachet d’eau fraîche à la main, il en avale une gorgée sous le regard impatient de ses passagers, déjà installés dans le car rapide stationné près de la station Elton. Il poursuit ses reproches sur l’état de la voie : « Nous ne pouvons pas passer notre temps à faire des déviations. Lorsqu’il pleut, c’est encore pire, tous nos moteurs finissent par être endommagés. » Au marché HLM, le bruit des marchandages se mêle au concert incessant des klaxons. Dans ce décor animé, Mamadou Cissé, conducteur de moto-jakarta vêtu du maillot d'un club européen, s’est installé confortablement sur sa monture pour observer le trafic. Il s’insurge : « L’État devrait vraiment nous venir en aide en reconstruisant cette route. Elle est impraticable, or nous ne pouvons pas rester sans travailler. Quand il pleut, Dieu seul sait à quel point il est difficile de traverser. » Les plaintes se multiplient de toutes parts, particulièrement chez ceux qui empruntent ce trajet quotidiennement. C’est le cas de Serigne Afia Mbacké, commerçant au marché HLM, PDG d’Afia HLM et automobiliste. Vêtu d’un costume africain et assis au volant de sa voiture noire de marque Nissan, il est visiblement pressé de démarrer. Il prend néanmoins quelques minutes pour détailler les conséquences de cette dégradation : « Les nids-de-poule provoquent constamment des accidents. Par exemple, un motocycliste peut tomber directement dans un trou, ou une voiture peut dévier pour en éviter un et percuter une moto ou un autre véhicule. On s’en sort systématiquement avec des dégâts. » Cet axe Colobane – HLM illustre ainsi parfaitement le quotidien des Dakarois : une population dynamique qui s'adapte en permanence aux défis de la ville. Mise au point du maire des HLM, Moustapha Diop Du côté des autorités compétentes, la réalité est tout autre. Les routes sont certes dégradées et impraticables, mais la municipalité ne ménage pas ses efforts pour tenter de réhabiliter la voirie. Moustapha Diop, maire des HLM, apporte des explications. Il commence d’abord par reconnaître l'état critique de certaines rues : « Aux HLM, nous reconnaissons qu’il y a énormément de routes qui sont en mauvais état. » Le maire avoue ensuite l'insuffisance criante du budget communal, ce qui rend la réfection des routes impossible à sa seule échelle : « Il faut comprendre la réalité de nos budgets : nos communes sont très petites et nous avons zéro ressource pour reprendre ou refaire une route. On ne va pas tourner autour du pot, nos budgets sont très, très insuffisants. » Conscient de ses prérogatives, il rappelle que la mairie a déjà saisi la Ville de Dakar : « Au niveau départemental, c'est la Ville de Dakar qui a la charge des routes. À plusieurs reprises, nous les avons alertés, relancés et leur avons envoyé la liste de nos priorités. Pourtant, cela fait quatre ans que nous attendons que la Ville de Dakar vienne enfin commencer à réhabiliter une route aux HLM, ce qui n'a pas encore été fait. » Au-delà des compétences de la Ville de Dakar, certaines voies dites « classées » relèvent de la responsabilité de l'État par le biais de l'Ageroute : « Aujourd'hui, le blocage concerne les axes majeurs restants, à commencer par la route principale du marché des HLM. C'est une route classée, ce qui signifie qu'elle appartient à l'État et qu'il lui revient de la reprendre complètement. De plus, c'est une route structurante, un axe d'urgence absolu où transitent et gravitent près de 50 000 personnes chaque jour pour aller au marché ou rejoindre Dakar. Les populations y passent, et les secousses du quotidien rendent cette réhabilitation urgente », explique le maire. Malgré ces difficultés, Moustapha Diop tient à nuancer la situation : « Cependant, il faut être juste : la commune des HLM est peut-être l'une des mieux loties. À part deux, trois ou quatre axes au maximum, la grande majorité de nos routes ont été totalement reprises et refaites par l'ONAS grâce au programme de renouvellement. » En guise de conclusion, il n’a pas manqué de lancer un appel pressant aux autorités compétentes : « Face à cette situation, nous relançons l'État et la Ville de Dakar pour que cette route structurante puisse enfin être restaurée. Nos administrés n'attendent que ça. » La patate chaude refilée à la ville de Dakar Alors que l'état des infrastructures routières suscite des débats dans plusieurs quartiers de la capitale, notamment aux HLM, la Ville de Dakar apporte des clarifications sur sa gestion de la voirie. Face aux critiques évoquant une absence d'interventions sur le réseau communal, M. Ansoumane Bayo, futur nouveau directeur des services techniques de la Ville de Dakar apporte des éclaircissements : « La ville de Dakar est intervenue au niveau des HLM, plus précisément un peu en haut des du marché, Sur cette partie-là, on a fait des travaux de pavage. Et si vous regardez aussi du côté de Castors vers le Rond-point Castors tout à fait à droite, là aussi il y a des interventions de la ville de Dakar.Au niveau de l’église Saint-Maurice Danger qui est sur la route principale, là aussi on vient récemment avec l'inscription du budget de la mairie de faire l'aménagement de cette partie de de cette église. » Pour comprendre la répartition des responsabilités à Dakar, M. Ansoumane Bayo rappelle qu'il existe une distinction claire entre deux types de voies : « on intervient sur toute la ville de Dakar en termes de pavage, en termes de réhabilitation de la chaussée mais tout ce qui est du périmètre communal, c'est-à-dire tout ce qui est voirie urbaine, tout ce qui est voirie communale. Voilà. Donc, il est prévu c'est un nouveau marché qui va bientôt démarrer avec de nouvelles entreprises et dans le la programmation qu'on va faire, il y aura véritablement la part de de la commune des HLM qui sera bien entendu prise en compte dans ce programme comme toutes les autres communes. Il y a aussi les routes classées qui s’inscrivent dans le domaine de l’état, c’est à l’Ageroute de s’en charger. » S'agissant des perspectives d'avenir, la Ville de Dakar annonce la fin d'un cycle contractuel triennal et le lancement imminent d'un tout nouveau programme d'aménagement et de réhabilitation de la voirie. Ce marché, dont les entreprises attributaires sont déjà désignées, couvrira l'ensemble des 19 communes du département de Dakar, y compris l'île de Gorée et la commune des HLM : « le marché est lancé, les entreprises attributaires sont connues et donc ce qui reste à faire, c'est véritablement démarrer les géologies, c'est démarrer les travaux mais bon, aussi avec les travaux des JOJ qui sont là aussi, je pense que c'est peut-être que ce sera juste après les JOJ que ces travaux vont commencer, ces marchés vont commencer. », annone Ansoumane Bayo. Parlant sous la supervision de M Birame Diop actuel directeur du développement urbain de la ville de dakar qui affirme prendre bientôt sa retraite, M Bayo s’explique sur l’axe rond-point colobane-marché HLM : « c'est l'avenue Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba. Ça, c'est une route classée. C'est une route classée donc c'est l'Ageroute qui y intervient généralement. Mais parfois il peut arriver des situations où la ville peut intervenir voilà pour soulager les populations. Comme il est arrivé récemment au niveau de Niarry Tally au niveau des deux voies de Niarry Tally qui commencent au niveau du rond-point Cices Bourguiba pour aller au terminal Liberté 5 qui est en cours en ce moment. » Fatou NGOM

items.title: Le Tunisia Podcasts Festival revient après trois ans d’absence
items.description: Podcast Days, le Tunisia Podcasts Festival, se tiendra à Tunis les vendredi 6 et samedi 7 novembre 2026 : une journée, deux soirées, deux lieux, à l’auditorium de l’Institut français de Tunisie (IFT), puis à L’Art Rue (Dar Bach Hamba), dans la médina, pour célébrer la création sonore sous toutes ses formes. Au programme : rencontres, masterclasses, tables-rondes, enregistrements publics et expériences immersives. L’entrée est libre, sur inscription . En décembre 2023, la première édition du Tunisia Podcasts Festival réunissait pendant trois jours podcasteurs, auditeurs et professionnels à B7L9 Art Station et à l’Espace L’Artisto. Trois ans après, un rendez-vous plus resserré. Les Podcast Days en gardent l’esprit, dans un format plus court : une soirée d’ouverture, une journée dense, une soirée de clôture. Mais l’événement s’inscrit dans la continuité, avec, cette année, des invités venus d’Alger et de Marseille. «Le podcast tunisien a beaucoup grandi depuis 2023. Il a trouvé ses voix, ses publics, parfois même ses modèles. Avec les Podcast Days, nous voulions lui offrir un lieu pour se rencontrer, apprendre, et regarder ce qui se fait de l'autre côté de la Méditerranée» , a déclaré Raouia Kheder, fondatrice du Tunisia Podcasts Festival. I. B. L’article Le Tunisia Podcasts Festival revient après trois ans d’absence est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Le calvaire du petit Sékouba, 18 mois, atteint d’une grave pathologie oculaire (attention, image sensible)
items.description: Il a 18 mois, il ne voit plus et hurle de douleur dès que la nuit tombe. Originaire de Sangbarala, dans la préfecture de Kouroussa, le petit Sékouba Condé souffre depuis sa naissance d'une maladie qui déforme progressivement ses yeux. Faute de moyens pour financer une évacuation sanitaire recommandée vers la Tunisie, sa famille lance un SOS au Président Mamadi Doumbouya et aux personnes de bonne volonté. C'est sa grand-mère, Mariama Camara, qui a saisi notre rédaction ce mercredi à Kankan. Les larmes aux yeux, elle raconte le calvaire quotidien de son petit-fils. D'une tache blanche à la cécité Tout serait parti d'un signe anodin. Une petite tache blanche sur les yeux à la naissance, sans douleur apparente. « Mon petit-fils est né avec cette maladie. Au début, il avait une tache blanche sur les yeux, mais cela ne lui faisait pas mal. Avec le temps, la maladie a évolué et les douleurs ont commencé. Une grosse boule s’est progressivement formée sur ses yeux, au point qu’il ne voit plus rien », confie Mariama Camara. Aujourd'hui, à un an et six mois, Sékouba ne supporterait plus que le paracétamol comme seul antalgique. « Quand il ne souffre pas, il joue et mange normalement. Mais dès que les douleurs commencent, nous ne dormons pas de toute la nuit, parfois jusqu’au petit matin. Il ne fait que crier : Grande mère… Grande mère… », poursuit-elle. De Kankan à Macenta, un parcours sans issue Pour tenter de sauver la vue de l'enfant, la famille a parcouru des centaines de kilomètres. De Kankan, où on leur conseille de se rendre à Conakry, à la capitale où les médecins confirment la présence d'une masse oculaire, jusqu'à Macenta où une radiographie est réalisée. « À Macenta, après la radiographie, ils nous ont dit d’aller en Tunisie. C’est ce que nous voulons faire, mais nous n’avons pas les moyens financiers nécessaires », explique la grand-mère. L'espoir d'une prise en charge spécialisée à l'étranger se heurte désormais au manque total de ressources. Un appel à la solidarité nationale Désemparée, Mariama Camara en appelle directement aux plus hautes autorités du pays. « Je tends la main au Président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, à son gouvernement et à toutes les personnes de bonne volonté. Au nom de Dieu et de son Prophète, nous leur demandons de nous venir en aide. Mon petit-fils a besoin d’aide, mais nous n’avons pas les moyens. Pour l’amour de Dieu, aidez-nous à soigner cet enfant. » En attendant une hypothétique prise en charge, le petit Sékouba reste à Sangbarala, dépendant de la solidarité pour accéder à des soins ophtalmologiques d'urgence dont son pronostic visuel dépend désormais. Karifa Kansan Doumbouya, correspondant régional – Kankan +224-612-51-22-79 L’article Le calvaire du petit Sékouba, 18 mois, atteint d’une grave pathologie oculaire (attention, image sensible) est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Stop the Bloodshed: Pyrates demands action from Tinubu, Kefas in Taraba
items.description: The National Association of Seadogs (Pyrates Confraternity) demanded decisive action from President Bola Tinubu and the Taraba State governor, Agbu Kefas, over the killing of at least 58 people in Binari community in Karim Lamido Local Government Area. The group also tasked security agencies to discontinue all peace arrangements that have enabled terror groups to rearm. The NAS Cap’n, Dr Charles Meribole, in a statement entitled ‘’ The Taraba Massacre: Another Bloodbath in Our Nation, ” condemned what he called ‘’senseless killings’’ of Nigerians, noting that it was ‘’barbaric, reprehensible and must not go unpunished “ Meribole, while mourning the dead, expressed disappointment with the response of Nigeria’s political leadership and the security agencies to recurring killings, especially in Northern Nigeria. He lamented that the over 20,000 Nigerians who have been killed since May 29, 2023, when President Tinubu assumed office, should jolt the President to rise to the full weight of his office as President and Commander-in- Chief of the Armed Forces and end Nigeria’s security crisis. ‘’President Bola Tinubu should recognise that the security of Nigerians is not a peripheral issue to be addressed when convenient or tackled with political rhetoric. It is a central test of his administration’s responsibility to Nigerians and obligation to his oath of office. ‘’ We implore President Bola Tinubu to translate his directives to the security agencies into measurable results. His orders to dismantle criminal networks must come with clear timelines, effective monitoring and consequences for failure. Those implementing security operations must be held accountable for their performance, and any official found to have compromised these efforts must face the appropriate consequences.’’ Meribole upbraided Kefas for attending the All Progressives Congress 2027 Presidential campaign (APC) North-West campaign flag-off, noting that traumatised people of Binari deserve empathy and not empty promises. He called on the security agencies to discharge their duties with renewed determination, stressing that since terror groups have demonstrated that they are remorseless, they should be treated with equal measure through sustained and decisive security operations. The statement read in part ‘’ President Bola Tinubu’s recent marching orders to dismantle terrorists and bandits’ enclaves, rescue kidnapped citizens and restore public confidence in the government’s capacity to protect lives and property must be pursued with sustained commitment. ‘’ There must be no retreat, no complacency and no room for compromise with those who terrorise innocent Nigerians. Any peace arrangement that enables criminal groups to regroup, rearm or continue their heinous crimes must be urgently discontinued where it undermines public safety. Criminal groups that repeatedly exploit peaceful overtures to perpetuate violence must be confronted through lawful, effective and sustained security operations. ‘’Terror groups have demonstrated that they are remorseless; they should be treated with equal measure. The war against terror groups must be waged with the seriousness it deserves until Nigerians can once again live without fear in their only country.’’ The post Stop the Bloodshed: Pyrates demands action from Tinubu, Kefas in Taraba appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: La Bourse de Casablanca démarre en baisse
items.description: La Bourse de Casablanca a démarré en baisse jeudi, son indice phare, le MASI, reculant de 0,15% à 16.901,2 points (pts). Le MASI 20, qui regroupe les 20 valeurs les plus liquides, gagnait 0,04% à 1.226,53 pts, tandis que le MASI ESG, indice des entreprises ayant la meilleure notation ESG selon Moody’s ESG Solutions, perdait 0,06% à 1.255,7 pts. Aux valeurs individuelles, les plus fortes baisses étaient accusées par Sanlam Maroc (-5,21% à 2.801 DH), Fenie Brossette (-2,26% à 303 DH), Mutandis (-1,81% à 217 DH), Disty Technologies (-1,76% à 335 DH) et TGCC S.A (-1,24% à 627 DH). En revanche, S.M Monétique (+5,21% à 505 DH), Stroc Industrie (+4,77% à 162,45 DH), SMI (+4,01% à 5.970 DH), Jet Contractors (+3,94% à 1.610 DH) et Afriquia Gaz (+3,4% à 3.619 DH) enregistraient les plus fortes hausses.
